maintopic: TRAFFIC AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES.
TRAFFIC AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
Before the orders of the day are called I would like to draw the attention of the Prime Minister or the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) to ah article which appears in the February issue of the ' Review of Reviews,' with reference to an agreement said to have been reached between the Railway Commission of Canada and the Interstate Commerce Commission of the United States. The article is as follows:
It is expected that with the reciprocity treaty there will also be submitted to Congress the text of some sort of traffic agreement with Canada to regulate railroad business over the border. . . . The report of Chairman Knapp, concurred in by Chairman Mabee, and presented to the Secretary of State on the last day of December, contains recommendations of such importance to those of our citizens who are interested in trade and travel across

the border that we herewith summarize its most important points.
Then the article goes on:
The proposed treaty provides for a tribunal to enforce and administer its provisions to be known as the International Commerce Commission and which shall consist of four members, namely, the chairman of the Interstate Commerce Commission and the chief commissioner of the Board of Kailway Commissioners of Canada for the time being, a member of the Interstate Commerce Commission to be appointed by the President of the United States, and a member of the Railway Commissioners of Canada to be appointed by the Governor General of Canada in Council. The powers conferred upon and the authority given to this commission in respect of international carriers would correspond to those exercised by the Interstate Commerce Commission in respect of interstate carriers within the United States.
The provisions of such a treaty should apply to telegraph, telephone and express companies and such companies should be subject as respect to international business to the authority of the International Commerce Commission.
I would like to point to a paragraph taken from the message of President Taft with reference, to reciprocity, which he sent to Congress on the 26th January last. After reciting a few of the matters which had been settled, and which, he says, enabled them to make a reciprocity agreement, he proceeds thus:
An equitable arrangement has recently been reached between our Interstate Commerce Commission and the similar body in Canada m regard to through rates on the transportation lines between the two countries. The path having been thus opened for the improvement oi commercial relations, a reciprocal trade agreement is the logical sequence of all that lias been accomplished in disposing of matters of a diplomatic and controversial character.
I would like to know if that be true, and if such an agreement has been reached between our Board of Railway Commissioners, and the Interstate Commerce Commission of the United States. If so, by whom was the initiative taken; and if such an agreement has been made, will it be submitted to this House before the conclusion of the discussion on reciprocity, as is proposed to be done apparently on the other side oT the line. Have our Railway Commissioners the authority to make any such agreement without subjecting it to ratification by this House? The whole trend of such an agreement, I presume, is to facilitate traffic north and south instead of east and west.

maintopic: TRAFFIC AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: As I have already stated on several occasions in this House, the question of control of rates on lines running from Canada into the United States, and from the United States into Canada

maintopic: TRAFFIC AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: has been under consideration, I think, more than a year. I am not prepared to say just who originated the idea of solving the problem by the appointment of an international tribunal. It was first brought to my attention by Judge Mabee, the chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada. The difficulties experienced by shippers on traffic between the two countries are quite apparent at times. For instance, the rate is a point, say from New York to Toronto. It is possible, I presume to get a through rate by the boards acting separately. But what results often is this, that the railway companies on each side charge a local tariff, particularly if there be no competition, and as a result the purchaser of the goods in Toronto is obliged to pay two local rates instead of one through rate. The object of the agreement, if one could be arrived at, was to form some tribunal that could quickly make a through rate that would apply from any point in Canada to any point in the United States and vice versa, so that, so far as control of rates was concerned, there would be a tribunal that as completely controlled the traffic originating in either country going to the other as if the traffic were all in one country. Judge Mabee and Mr. Knapp, head of the Interstate Commerce Commission, had several conferences and they did arrive at a basis that to them seemed satisfactory for the solution of the difficulty, and in a manner to protect both shippers and producers on either side of the line having business on the other side. The report of each of these gentlemen is now in the hands of his government. If approved it will take the form of a treaty. As to the details, so far as I am concerned, they have not been given to the public. But the information which my hon. friend (Mr. Middlebro) finds in the magazine referred to approximates the truth as to outlining the details. All I can say is, that so far as the Canadian government is concerned, this matter is still under consideration, and no action has yet been taken. But the report of Judge Mabee was made to this government as the report of Mr. Knapp was made to the United States government.

maintopic: TRAFFIC AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Did Mr. Mabee take the initiative in this matter without any consultation with or authorization from the government?

maintopic: TRAFFIC AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: No, that is not what I said. I said I was not in a position to say who originally took the initiative; the first I heard of it, Judge Mabee discussed it with me, and he had full authority to discuss it with Mr. Knapp and make a report embodying their views.	[DOT]

maintopic: TRAFFIC AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
This report, apparently, states that an agreement will be sub-

mitted to the United States Congress when the treaty is discussed. Will it be discussed here when we discuss reciprocity?

maintopic: TRAFFIC AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: It will be premature, 1 imagine, to say much about it, as it is entirely under negotiation at the present time. And, as it will be in the form of a treaty, the usual custom and practice as to treaties will be followed in both countries.

House again in committee on Bill (No. 70) respecting the Canadian Western Railway Company.-Mr. Turriff.
On section 1,

This company has a local charter covering almost identically the same ground and the condition has been imposed that they must build thirty miles of the road within one year. Would the Minister of Railways and Canals think it proper to restrict the Dominion charter in the same manner as it might have a tendency to expedite the work?
How long has the provincial charter been in existence?
About three years.
Have they built any of the thirty miles?
They have had the charter renewed once.

The difficulty about a clause of that kind is that it does not have any effect in making them build. You say that they must build a certain number of miles within a limited time, but the only result has been that they come back and ask for a renewal just the same as if there'had not been any condition of the kind. It is a difficult question to determine how to induce the railway companies to build a little more rapidly than they are doing. My own private opinion is that no clause of this kind will make them build a mile of railway any quicker. When the railway company want to build they will do it. The only alternative is not to renew their charter if such a renewal is interfering with the construction of a railway. The fact that this company came back for a renewal of the local charter instead of building thirty miles of road within a year, proves that the imposition of that condition did not result in expediting the railway. I suggested once or twice to railway companies that we would have to impose some such condition and they said: All right, do not renew the charter for we will only have to come back for another renewal; we cannot build the road in the time stipulated. If my hon. friend wants to do something practical in order to get the railway constructed I am afraid such a clause as he suggests will not accomplish
legitimate excuse for asking for another renewal. It is getting to be a perfect humbug to put in conditions which are never observed and which the companies do not intend to observe at the time they accept a renewal, and largely the members of the committee, I believe as a rule, and the Minister of Railways, judging from the result, do not intend to hold the company to the condition at the time. It is getting to be more or less of a scandal. Year after year we are granting these renewals and it is thoroughly well known that railway companies snap their fingers at us and that we have no way of enforcing the conditions imposed by us. If we cancelled a few of the charters, or if we refused to renew them, we would have a different condition of things altogether.

SINCLAIR (Guysborough), moved:'
That in the opinion of this House, as the mode of fishing known as steam trawling, prosecuted by ships of different nationalities on the coast of Canada outside Canadian waters, is destructive to fish life, it is expedient, in order to conserve the deep sea fisheries, that negotiations be opened with the view of securing an international agreement prohibiting this mode of fishing in such spawning grounds for deep sea fish, as the waters of the Gulf of St. Lawrence and the banks of the North Atlantic adjacent to the coasts of Canada and Newfoundland.
He said:	My purpose in moving this
resolution is to press upon parliament, and especially upon the government, the importance of dealing with this question. I bring it forward with a good deal of confidence, knowing that in the past the government have not given any encouragement or assistance to this mode of fishing. When this matter was first discussed on the coast of Nova Scotia some few years ago, the fishery committee of the Halifax Board of Trade pressed upon the government the importance, in their view, of doing something in the way of in-trcducing this mode of fishing in Canadian waters. The request they made on that occasion was met with prompt refusal from the Alinister of Marine

Having carefully followed the fishing operations carried on by steam trawlers on hoard the trawler 'Wren/ I hare to report that the complaints made against such operations are entirely without just reason. On the contrary, instead of being exceedingly destructive and wasteful, practically everything drawn up in the great net, excepting the dogfish which are entangled in considerable numbers, is utilized and turned to account, and the very destruction of the dogfish is a benefit, whilst the men are entitled to save their livers on their own behalf. I understand that until recently the flat fishes, such as the rougli-dab, were thrown away; but since the establishment of the glue factory at Canso such are now sold to that institution. There is really nothing drawn up in the net which any economical fishing corporation would ever think of wasting, and certainly the captain of the 'Wren' is awake to the interests of the Maritime Fish Corporation in this respect. The bulk of the fish caught is haddock, and it is for them that the trawling is carried on. The weight of the catch of haddock was 27,580 pounds, exclusive of 3,300 pounds of assorted small ones. This numerically, judging by the respective sizes, approximately represents some 6,895 and 1,650 fish. The weight of flat fishes was 325 pounds, of the cod, 150 pounds, and of the hake, 1,550 pounds, or numerically, 100 flat fishes, 25 cod and 100 hake. True, I was dependent on the corporation for these figures after landing at Canso; but based on^my own observations on 'board the 'Wren/ I can vouch for the figures being approximately correct. The total weight of these was 32/105 pounds, and the number approximately 8,770. Besides them, leaving out the dogfish, there were a few silver hake, pollock, skate and gaspereau. and a shad, an angler, and an eel. It is difficult to form an estimate of the number of dogfish caught, but the number was very considerable. Sometimes there would be only two or three, and at other times the net seemed to have swept through a regular school of them; and they are immediately destroyed, their livers cut out and thrown overboard. Besides the true fishes there were a very limited number of squid, saved like other odds and ends, like the angler, skates, &c., for making glue, and there were hardly any other invertebrates except a few worthless star fishes, Ac. I will work the matter out in a more detailed way later, but meanwhile give some broad outlines in a summary way. Occasionally, but very rarely, I saw an insignificant gaspereau or other very small fish thrown overboard; but there is virtually no waste whatsoever. The operations were carried on not closer to the land than four miles, and besides the 'Coquette* no other fishing craft was to be seen.

The fourth point I make is that trawling depletes the fishing grounds. It follows that if large quantities of undersized fish are taken that will naturally deplete the grounds. I am quite aware that this is also disputed. For example the Fish Traders' ' Gazette,' of London, which is looked upon as one of the most influential papers in the trade in the world, published a few days ago a statement referring to the fishing industry in the past year, from which I shall quote one paragraph :
It is not expected that the weight of the fish caught will show any appreciable change either* way or the other when the official figures are available, but it is noted with satisfaction that many of the North Sea grounds have produced improved supplies; while several new though restricted areas for trawling have been discovered by local fishermen.

Cowie, in the report of the Fisheries Department for the year 1910, says that steam trawling has not had the effect of depleting the North Sea. I wish to say a few words on that statement, ibut let me read what he did say so as to avoid any misunderstanding. Here is Mr. Cowie's statement ;
I have always maintained in the press and otherwise, that trawling within limited sea areas is most destructive, and, apart from the fact that the many line fishermen, who depend for a living entirely on what the baited line captures, have some rights, held that the compelling of the steam trawler to keep to the open sea and the offshore grounds is a wise and necessary measure for the protection and insurance of the fish supply, from inshore grounds.	.
At the same time, I cannot agree with those who assert that trawling, if long continued offshore, as well as inshore, is destined to deplete the sea of food fishes.
Notwithstanding the alarming prognostications of a- sea denuded of fish life, and ruined and idle line-fishing fleets, put forth at the recent international conference at Washington, United States of America, as the results expected to attend the use of the otter trawl on the Atlantic ' banks ', the facts and figures concerning trawling in the comparatively narrow North Sea, where the method is so oid, and the fleets so large, do not at all lend themselves to such alarmist views.

The fishermen do not come here as suppliants, they do not ask for any special favour, all they ask is that they will get a square deal for themselves and for the business by which they make a living. The fishermen of Canada have been accustomed to look after themselves The method that has been adopted in this country in regard to this industry for generations by which the fisherman is captain of his own vessel and master and owner of his own business has tended to produce a virile and robust type of men. If you, Mr. Speaker, and other hon. members of this House, could see, as I have seen, the fishermen engaged in winter fishing on the coasts of my own constituency, on a winter morning, when the thermometer is around zero and the whitecaps are on the water, steering in open boats for the open sea to spend the day in the prosecution of their calling, regardless of the cold, regardless of the sudden gales prevailing in those stormy waters, you would understand the force of my statement that this line of business tends to produce a virile and robust type of men. During the last few years a good deal of oratory has been indulged in in regard to the importance of maintaining the naval supremacy of the British Empire. Let me say that the best contribution we can make here in Canada to the naval supremacy of the empire is to stand by our fishermen.
I venture to say that no other part of the British Empire, or, I think I could say no other part of the world, can produce a finer or more robust body of seamen than the men who tramp the decks of our fishing vessels. These men are hardy and adventurous ; nor are they lacking in courage. Every year adds to the list of brave deeds done by these men who frequent our coast waters engaged in the fishing industry. Permit me to give an example recently published in the Boston ' Post ' :
Every now and then a splendid deed is done that makes the sun seem very bright and life well worth living in this throat-throttling era of competition.
Every athletic profession has its opportunities for heroic daring, but possibly none greater than those who go down to the sea in little vessels. Here the Gloucester fishermen have an enviable record.
The other day, a sailor on the fishing schooner ' Athlete ' was swept into the sea while trying to secure a sail in a howling gale. To breast the waves in a dory seemed the madness of suicide, but in a minute the crew was engaged in a desperate struggle to see who should man the rescuing dory. Two sturdy fishermen won out and managed to launch the shell. The man they tried to save was found dead, killed by floating wreckage. With the greatest difficulty the heroes regained their schooner.

Such a defiance to danger and death makes the blood of all men run redder and beat quicker. There is no need of pessimism when we breed such men.
Similar incidents of bravery of this kind can be told in connection with a blizzard that took place on tire coast of Nova Scotia on the 6th of January last year when the little haddock fleet at Dover and Whitehead was driven to sea in a wintry gale, and when tossed by the storm, the sails frozen and the vessels accumulating ice until they were almost ready to sink, brave men risked their lives to save their comrades. A. B. in July, 1909. Mr. Sullivan will receive the bronze medal, which is emblematic of the highest honour for bravery which the Drench government bestows upon a civilian. I do not know why this medal came through the United States government, but probably this man was working on board an American ship at the time. Stories like the foregoing are told around the firesides in Nova Scotia every year on the return of the Banking fleet. The record of many of these vessels carrying on this hazardous business has been handed down from father to son for generations. Year after year the hungry sea claims its toll. Every spring the sailors leave with high hopes, and the best of good cheer, but when the storms and the fog have done their work some of the ships are sure to return with flags at half-mast. Our (people have paid dearly for their proprietary rights in these Bank fisheries, and the families are very few on the coast of Nova Scotia who have not lost relatives in these waters. Not even the miners follow a more hazardous calling- It has been said that it costs a life for every 100,000 tons of coal mined, and the fish we eat must be won at an equally dreadful price.
Now, we are deeply interested in this matter in the maritime provinces, -because we not only man our own fleet but, to a large extent, that of New England as well, and it would be a calamity to the maritime provinces if anything should happen to drive the bank fishermen off the sea. No nation ever yet became a great maritime power without first building up its fisheries. The fishing fleet of Great Britain is to-day the greatest fishing fleet in the world, and it is the basis of Britain's naval power and her commercial sea-power as

well. Canada owns to-day the greatest fisheries to be found in the world, and the question is whether we can preserve and hand them down to those who come after us. I am stating it mildly when I say that our fishermen are alarmed at the influence this mode of fishing is likely to have on their business-not only the deep sea fishermen hut the inshore fishermen as well. I had the honour, last year, to present petitions signed toy 1,800 fishermen on the coast of my county who are in sympathy with the deep sea fishermen on this question. Resolutions have come from fishermen's unions and associations all along the coast asking that some action be taken in regard to this matter. I do not regard this as unnecessary or needless alarm. The depletion of the fisheries is, of course, the most important thing. I know that it will be contended that it is necessary to prosecute this mode of fishing in order to keep up the constant supply in the market. It is also contended that the sea is large, and that no method of fishing that we can adopt will destroy the fish. It is true, the Atlantic ocean embraces a very large area, but it must not be forgotten that those portions of it frequented by fish, and where the fish shed their spawn embrace a comparatively small area, and so it is quite possible, by improvident methods of fishing to destroy the fishery. International conventions have taken place for the purpose of conserving the forests and our other natural resources of this continent. International arrangements are now in force to protect tire sealing industry of the coast of Alaska. I submit that the best breeding ground of cod-fish and haddock in the world is important enough to call for international negotiations to settle this question of steam trawling. I submit, that we should, without delay, endeavour to obtain some arrangement by which we can secure an international agreement prohibiting trawling in the spawning grounds, which, I take to be the Gulf of St. Lawrence and the Banks. I have no way of saying how these regulations could ibe secured, but I think that it could be done. The United States, I understand, is in the same position as ourselves, and the sympathy of the government at Washington ought to be with the Canadian government in respect to this matter, they having a large fishing fleet on th© sea which is disturbed as ours is, by this method of fishing. It is not for me to dictate to the governments of Canada and the United States, but, as they are equallv concerned, if thev will act together, they should be able to secure such international arrangements as will preserve this great industry, and do justice to the men who 'are engaged in it.

Mr. Speaker, coming from the maritime prov-98
inces as. I do, and representing a county with 90 miles of coast line or so off which is one of the best fishing grounds in Canada, I need not apologize to the House for taking up a little of the time devoted to this discussion. My hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) has gone so ably and exhaustively into the discussion of this matter that it might be supposed that it should be content with simply expressing my acquiescence in what he has said. But when I tell you that this trawler, the 1 Wren,' has been operating off the coast of Antigonisli for a portion of each season for three years past, which operations have been much to the dissatisfaction and injury of local fishermen, I make bold to hope you will excuse me if I presume to discuss this matter at a little greater length, and even though, in discussing it I should find it necessary to go over again some of the ground covered by my hon. friend.
The importance of the fisheries is generally recognized. We are spending hundreds and thousands of dollars every year in endeavours to conserve our natural resources. We spend large sums in the protection of our fisheries, in the establishment of hatcheries, and a dozen of ways to promote our fisheries. In the city of Quebec a meeting was held a few days ago of eminent Canadians and others to advocate the conservation of our natural resources. They are doing a great work. I claim that in the fisheries of Canada we have the greatest heritage that any country ever possessed ; and it is the duty of this government and of the Canadian people to see that that heritage is handed down to posterity without any serious diminution. There is an idea prevalent among the fishermen, and indeed among us all, that we are justified in taking present advantage of every opportunity to utilize the natural resources in which our country abounds, and without having any consideration for the future. That sentiment I submit is an unfair and a dishonest one. The idea prevails that we have a right to get all we can out of our fisheries, irrespective of future results. We hear it sometimes said : What has posterity done for us? We will make-all we can out of our present resources. As I have said, I think that is an unworthy and unpatriotic sentiment. I claim it is the duty of the government to take steps to conserve these valuable fisheries, and that we should transmit them unimpaired as we received them.
My hon. and learned friend (Mr. Sinclair), has gone over the history of trawling pretty well. He has informed the House that there are over 3,000 of these trawlers operating in the North Sea. We hear the argument made sometimes that since these trawlers have been operating on the coast of Great Britain for a period of 125 years, there cannot be any very



serious or harmful results from trawling. 1 propose to trace the history of trawling in the old country, and to call your attention to some investigations that have been held by the authorities, and to show the evolution of opinion that has been going on in the old country with respect to trawling.
I should also quote the findings of royal commissions, appointed to investigate this matter, and show how opinion has changed with regard to the matter. I do not quote these resolutions, .because I endorse the views therein contained so far as they may be an apology for, or defence of trawling. At the same time they were expressed, there was a strong approval of the custom ; *but as time rolled on, and as the number of trawlers increased, that opinion seems to have changed in the old country. At that time trawling was pronounced to be ' the source of the greatest and most progressive supply of fish other than herring to the principal markets of the country.' To-day it is generally recognized that the practice of trawling has been injurious to the fishing industry, injurious both to the fisheries themselves and to the line fishermen. I may say that the shore fishermen have been practically driven out of business altogether. In the city of London, the proportion of fish caught by trawlers to that caught by hand lines, is something like 10 or 12 to one. The result of trawling has been that the line fishermen practically abandoned the field to their enemy, the trawler. Latterly, they have been making efforts to recover their ground in certain waters along the east coast of Scotland, and other parts of the United Kingdom, and the result is, that the line fishermen are now beginning to regain a part of what they have lost and are hopeful that in a short time they will be able to prosecute with advantage the industry that seemed once to have about disappeared. The history of trawling in the old country is the history of a prolonged fight between the line fishermen and the men engaged in this destructive method o,f fishing. The hostility of the line fishermen has been so great that it was scarcely safe for any prominent man to express any sympathy with the trawlers. There have been demonstrations against these trawlers in Aberdeen and other towns on the east coast of Scotland, and the way they took to show their hostility was to conclude their demonstrations with that irrefutable argument of burning in effigy any person to be in sympathy with the trawlers. Now I wish first to refer to a report of a royal commission that was published in 1863. It was appointed to investigate certain complaints of the fishermen who asserted that their industry was being destroyed, that the spawning grounds were injured, and that a large number of imma-Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonish).
ture fish -were caught, with the result that tlie fisheries were becoming exhausted and threatened with extinction. This commission was composed of such eminent men as the Kt. Hon. G. Shaw-Lefevbre, Sir James Caird and Prof. Huxley. Here is what they say regarding the waste 'by destruction :
Waste by the destruction of young fish takes place in the course of the practice of all modes of fishing, and is to a certain extent inseparable from them. The waste which occurs in the course of beam trawling in the open sea and in all kinds of sweep net fishing has certainly not affected the supply of fish in many localities, and is not proved to have affected it in any. With respect to inshore fishing, although the evidence so far as it is conclusive, appears to prove thaj. the taking of small and immature fish, has not as yet produced any serious effect upon the fisheries, it is undoubtedly possible that by improved engines the destruction of fry might reach such a pitch as to show a large, instead of as at present, an insignificant ratio to the destruction effected by the natural enemies and by conditions unfavourable to their existence.
That report was made in 1863, when trawling was not carried on to the same extent that it has been in later years. But even then you will observe that report states that, whilst it was denied that destruction was taking place, to any very appreciable extent, yet there is an admission that there is a great deal of waste; and a further admission that whilst the taking of small and immature fish has not as yet produced any serious effect upon the fishery, it is possible that such will be the result ultimately. Subsequent to 1863 other commissions reported, but I will only call attention to that which was appointed in 1883, the president of which was Lord Dalhousie. In this report the Royal Commission go on to say :
We are unable to come to the conclusion that trawling is the sole cause of the decrease of fish in inshore waters. In so far as it may contribute to any decrease, we think it can only be as part of a system of overfishing and not because of the wasteful destruction of spawn, fish food or immature fish.
There is an admission of injury; they admit that trawling produces a decrease in the quantity of fish, but they are unable to come to the conclusion that trawling is the sole cause of the decrease in the inshore fisheries. You will observe that the commission admit that there is a decrease in the inshore waters, that the decrease is noticeable, and that they attribute it to the system of over-fishing. I do not care what it is attributed t'o; what we are after is the result, and the result is that there has been a diminution in the quantity of fish. Blackwood's Magazine for May, 1885. has an article on this subject,. and the very fact that it is in Blackwood's Magazine justifies

me in quoting it. It refers to the report of the Trawling Commission of 1883 on the fish supply. There is a reference to the destruction of immature fish, but before I come to that I might refer to the destruction of spawn. One of the arguments used against the trawlers is the injury to the spawning ground and the destruction of spawn. According to the finding of the Royal Commission, that is not the case. The opinion that such is the case is based upon misapprehension, for it is a fact, that the spawn of fish generally is found, not upon the bottom, but floating on or very near the surface. The ripe uninjured ova of cod, halibut and most of fish is not found on the bottom. The principal exception to this is in the case of herring, the spawn of which goes to the bottom, so that the operations of the trawlers would not seriously affect the spawn. One would think they might, perhaps, affect the spawning ground, but the finding of the commission is that they do not seriously do so. There is a slight disturbance of the ground, but this is very temporary, and normal conditions are soon restored. Now, to come to the question of the destruction of immature fish, I find in this article in Blackwood's to which I have already referred, the following:
If evidence of reputation were to be trusted, the trawlers would come off badly on the charge of destroying immature fish. The had name that they have incurred in this respect is perhaps due to the work of the small trawlers alluded to in the beginning of this paper, who on many parts of the coast work iclose inshore, and probably do destroy a large amount of fry. Although, throughout the evidence taken by the commission, it is clearly the belief of the fishermen that this evil prevails to a very large extent, they do not seem to have produced any really conclusive proofs of its existence. ' In the experiments of Professor McIntosh

Prof. McIntosh is a professor of St. Andrews university, one of the greatest scientists of Scotland. He conducted a series of investigations from 1885 to 1895, in. a trawler placed at his disposal for the purpose, called the * Garland,' and wrote some works on the subject, one of them ' Resources of the Sea.' He is quite an authority on fish and the operations of trawlers.
-hi the experiments of Professor McIntosh, the immature fish registered as caught in the trawl were mostly of the less valuable hinds. The quantity of young haddock and whiting taken was inconsiderable, the immature specimens of these fishes being generally found in the mouths of the larger kinds a state of things that makes the trawlers their avengers rather than their murderers. It seems likely that below a certain size the fry escape altogether through l5eT fne^hes of the trawl-net, as Professor McIntosh states that it was rare to capture dabs under 51 inches in length, and that in using the small trawl close inshore in St.
Andrew's hay, none of the smaller fiat fishes with which that region abounds were taken. Tins absence of immature fish in large quantities from the trawl-net was fully borne out by the trawlers themselves; and it seems clear that, at any rate in the districts visited by the commission, there is no wasteful or unnecessary destruction of food-fishes committed in this way.
This refers to .the commission of 1883, and it would appear from reading it that the charge against the trawlers was very much exaggerated. As I said before, I 'do not agree that the charge that is made to-day against the trawlers is very much exaggerated, but if these assertions were made at that time 1 would think that they would be much exaggerated, because conditions have changed since then. The number trawlers then was comparatively lim-J' There was not the same intensity of fishing if 1 may so describe it, then as there is now. I am quoting this tor ^ the purpose of showing the change which has been going on with respect to trawling. My hon. friend from Guys-borough (Mr. Sinclair) referred to the report of Mr. Halkett to the effect that there has been no great destruction at all of fish m the operation of the ' Wr'en.' In that report it is claimed there is no real waste or destruction of fish except dog fish. I quite agree with the remarks of my hon friendf from Guysborough, and I cannot understand how Air. Halkett could arrive at such a conclusion. It does seem almost incredible that no small fish were found in the trawler on the occasion of Prof. Hal-kett's visit. It strikes me that Prof'. Halkett must have started out, well fortified by his instructions from the department, feeling as strong as Samson, but when he got on board the trawler he nfust have mel some Delilah, before whom he gave way. I do not think that the report of Prof. Halkett should be given very much credit now He may, when he works the thing out, as he promises in his interim report to do, be able _ to explain some of the seeming inconsistencies of the report. But he is not alone in his praise of trawlers. He has company in the person of Mr. Alexander Milliken, General Inspector of Fisheries for Scotland, who does not agree that trawling is a bad thing. With the case that has been made against the trawler, it is surprising that anybody can be got to defend it, but here is a man who not only defends it' but commends it. He says, in his report to the board m 1907:
Having in view the fact that these fish (referring to catfish, marks and other fishes) were rarely caught by lines, and their destructive powers amongst other fish such as herrings and haddocks, it can be seen what an immense benefit it is to the general prosperity of the fisheries to have such large quantities of these destructive fish captured annually ^\hich were formally allowed to roam at sea until they die of old age.

Thus Mr. Milliken seems to think that trawling is a good thing because it destroys some of those fish that roam the sea and kill fish that are of merchantable value.
I am sure none of our fishermen in Nova Scotia will adopt this view. This recalls to my mind the story of the Scotchman "and the bagpipes that was told in this House at the earlier part of the session by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark). A Scotchman was sick unto death, in the hospital and the doctor was called in. The doctor examined the phar-macopoea, but he could not find anything to suit the case. He decided upon a novel remedy and suggested that a Highlander be brought to play the_ bagpipes, walking up and down the hall in the ward beside the patient's room. Next morning the doctor returned to the house and met the nurse who looked very serious, and he said:	'How is Sandy?' The answer was:
4 Oh, Sandy is all right, but all the rest of the patients are dead.' This is very similar. Prof. Milliken would allow the trawlers to operate in order that they may destroy those voracious fish that roam the sea, but he forgets that the other fish are being interfered with and destroyed at the same time. In a word the trawler kills the hen that lays the golden egg. Now, I have read to you the report of the Royal Commission of 1863, and that of the Royal Commission of 1883. To summarize these reports: In the report of 1883 it was alleged that there had been a destruction of spawn. The finding was that such was not the case, that that allegation was based upon a false assumption, that false assumption not taking into account the fact that spawn, as a rule, float near the surface. Than there was the allegation of the destruction of immature fish. The finding was that there was no evidence of the wasteful destruction of immature food fishes. There was the allegation that there was a disturbance and exhaustion of fishing grounds. By disturbance I mean that the fish are frightened away from the fishing grounds or the fish go away for a shorter or longer period, but' that they may return later on. Exhaustion means that the grounds are fished out. As to disturbance and exhaustion, this report of the commission of 1883 finds that the number of fish in inshore and narrow seas may be seriously diminished by the use of trawlers. If in the narrower seas there is exhaustion because of the operations of trawlers, it naturally follows that in the broader seas, in the high seas, where you have a large number of trawlers operating, the same result, is inevitable. It is only a question 'of degree. Then there is the allegation that the injury done by the trawlers to the food of fish is insignificant.
A select committee on Sea Fisheries was Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonisli).
appointed in 1893. It was appointed ' to consider the expediency of adopting measures for the preservation and improvement of the sea fisheries in the seas off the British Isles including the prohibition of the capture, landing or sale of undersized sea fish
and other like regulations, international or otherwise.'
Evidently an impression was beginning to prevail among the fishermen and others that something was required for the preservation of the fisheries, that the fish were in danger. This committee proceeded with its investigation, and there seems to be great contradiction in the testimony of the witnesses who came before them. The evidence of those in the trade, those engaged in fishing with trawlers, conflicted with that of the professional and scientific witnesses in regard to the decrease in the quantity and size of fish caught in the North Sea. The naturalists of the Marine Biological Association, Messrs Holt and Calderwood, and other witnesses whose testimony was of a technical character maintained that there was a decided depletion in the North Sea fisheries. The evidence of those in the trade was to the effect that there was virtually no destruction, and no serious diminution in the quantity of fish. The finding of this committee was:
There is no indication of a falling off in the number of herrings to be found off our coasts.
There is no evidence of important diminution in cod and haddock.
A considerable diminution in flat fishes, as soles and plaice, which must be attributed to over fishing by trawlers in certain localities.
I cannot understand why there should be a finding with respect to herring, because they are not ground fish at all, and are not affected by trawling unless it might be that a decrease in the quantity of herring might follow an undue disturbance of the grounds where the bait was found.
In 1900 a select committee was appointed on the Fisheries Bill. They found:
That 'it is proved beyond doubt that there is a very serious diminution in the supply of certain kinds of flat flsh, particularly in the North Sea.
That in default of a remedy, the consequence to the flat-fish industry will be disastrous.
That one of the causes of this diminution of supply is undoubtedly the destruction of inshore fish.
The committee in the conclusion of their report UTged:
That the subject of the diminution of the fish supply is a very pressing one. That no efforts should be spared to arrange for international treatment of the subject generally.
Whilst in these reports it is denied that trawling particularly destroys spawn or wastes immature fish, or injures the spawning ground to any great extent so far as

the outer waters are concerned, yet it is admitted on all sides that in the inshore fisheries there has been a decrease both in quantity and quality.
I wish to call your attention to a finding in one of these reports with reference to the falling off in the bays and harbours where trawling has been largely carried on.
Continuous fishing with such an effective implement as the steam trawler within a limited area may sensibly diminish the number of fish.
_ Now, what occurs in the limited area is bound to happen in the broader area if you increase the number of those effective implements.
At the beginning of investigation made in 1883, a series of questions put to Coast Guard officers of the United Kingdom elicited answers that in 52 districts out of 85 there was a falling off in the quantity of fish taken and in 45 of these where there was falling off trawling in some shape carried on.
At Scarborough, Aberdeen and St. Andrews' catches fell off greatly pointing to danger of exhaustion if continued.
James Farquharson, fishery officer for Banff, in a report dated January 5, 1907, after stating that line fishing returns for that year compared favourably with those of previous year, adds that cod and haddock show a considerable increase in quantity and concludes:
, Fishermen are of opinion that the increase is partly due to the absence of trawlers in the Firth.
J ames Ritchie, Findhorn, district, in a report dated January 3, 1907, says:
There was little cod fishing done in the Moray Firth by line fishermen as that species ot fish was very scarce. Fishermen, however, are hopeful that the fishing may improve if trawling is prohibited in the Firth.
Inquiries in Denmark, Holland and Germany elicited the reply that they had like conditions.
I have before me extracts from the evidence taken before a special committee to inquire into the conditions of the fishing industry of the United Kingdom, under date of April 1, 1908. I find that Mr. G. Alward, connected with the fishing trade all_ his life, gave evidence. He lived at Grimsby since 1856. He was the owner of several fishing vessels, and was connected with National Sea Fisheries Protection Association for twenty years and member of the executive thereof the greater part of that time-an expert.
Q. Is it your opinion that the fact that you do find these small fish on the grounds where you previously got large fish is due to what we might call the intensity of fishing, the big fish having been killed?-A. That has something to do with it. Of course, in the North Sea, as you have probably had placed
before you, the theory put forward-and I think there is a great deal of truth in it, is that the reason why we get so many small fish on the east side is that the larvae float into it, driven by the currents, and find a suitable location, and live on, whilst in the middle of the North Sea, the probability is that a large portion never get into that side of the tide and die.
Q. (To Sir Reginald McLeod). Is it your impression there is a decrease in the quantity of fish -obtainable on the banks in the North Sea?-A. I think that is well established, and that it extends over many years -going back say thirty years.
Q. Would the fact that you have been able to maintain the fish supply be due to the circumstance that you are now fishing over a wider area, and with more elaborate and effective engines?-A. That is so.
Q. So you think some steps should be taken shortly-the sooner the better-to avoid intensity of fishing?-A. Well, some step-I do not know exactly what step you could talce unless you resort to those farther grounds, and that I think is what we are doing. Personally we are doing that now; we are drawing off froin the old grounds a number of those big ships and going to far-off grounds, so that we are giving the North Sea somewhat of a rest.
Q. And that rest, coupled with the checks which you have suggested of the destruction of immature fish, may effect the purpose in your opinion?-A. Yes, it may.
We lamented the foot that we were landing so much of that small fish and I think that induced us to be more severe on the question of stopping the catch.
These reports show clearly that during the past 25 years there has been a gradual change of opinion going on in the old country on this matter until a stage has now been reached when both the fishermen and the people generally are asking for measures to be taken for the protection of the fisheries. As the hon. member for Guys-borough has pointed out, the government has shown its sympathy with the shore fishermen in various ways. In the first place, when the Halifax Board of Trade asked that the government should assist in bringing out some of these trawlers from Scotland, the government promptly refused to do so. This is shown by the following letter from the late Minister of Marine and Fisheries, Hon. R. Prefontaine, to-Mr. C. H. Mitchell, the chairman of the Fisheries Committee of the Halifax Board of Trade, in reference to that proposal:
June 5, 1905.
Dear Sir,-Referring to the matter of the introduction of steam trawling in Atlantic waters of Canada, I have an official report before me, and I do not see that any encouragement could be field out to steam trawl firms to operate in our waters. You are no doubt aware that to that destructive method of fishing has been attributed the destruction of valuable fisheries off the shores of Great Britain, and prohibitory laws have been enforced in inshore areas.
Outside the three-mile limit trawling cannot be prevented, but I am not disposed to

favour it in territorial waters or grant assistance to firms adopting that mode of fishing.
Tours faithfully.

C. H. Mitchell, Esq.,
Wood's Wharf, Halifax, N.S.
This letter shows that the government, instead of encouraging the use of steam trawlers, has taken strong ground against them; and I am quite sure that if the Marine and Fisheries Department can go further than they have gone in restricting this method of fishing, it will do so. If the department has exhausted its jurisdiction in Canadian waters and trawling can still go on beyond the three-mile limit-and this is a matter that every constitutional lawyer must admit-then the only thing that remains is the adoption of some international regulations.
At six o'clock. House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

Before six o'clock, I was referring to the work of some of the Royal Commissions appointed to investigate this question of the destruction of fisheries by trawlers and drew attention to the change of public opinion in the old country regarding the destructive effects of steam trawling. I pointed out that, in the earlier days of the prosecution of the fishing industry by trawling there did not appear to be the same alarm as developed itself later. At present it is generally conceded that the system of steam trawling is a destructive one. It is admitted on all sides that the inshore fisheries have suffered considerably by reason of this method of fishing, and it is only a question of degree and to what extent it shall be allowed to go on until you have the same conditions in the outer waters as now exists in the inshore waters. In the old country, it is recognized to-day that there has been a great falling off in the inshore fishing, more than any one anticipated in the earlier days of steam trawling.
Objection may be made that the natural enemy of fish is the fish themselves and not men. It is quite true that we know comparatively little of the laws which govern the relations between the different species of fish and of the causes which produce the migration of fish at certain times and the gathering of them together in large shoals at other times, and which leads to the dispersion of these shoals at other periods. Nor do we know much of what becomes of the spawn, or what becomes of the fry, but it is admitted on all sides that the quantity of fish usually taken by man is infinitesimally small a3 compared with the destruction in the sea caused by the fish themselves prey-Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonish).
ing on one another. There is a continual warfare going on amongst the various species and descriptions of fish the one against the other. The moment the spawn is shed it is attacked by numerous small fish, then when it is hatched it is attacked by larger fish. Herring is attacked by the dog-fish and sharks. These are again attacked in turn by the various larger fish, and it is a case all around of the great feeding on the little. Still there is a proper proportion maintained and nature does provide for the maintenance of a proper equilibrium between the different classes; but when you go beyond the line and by artificial means interfere too much with nature, the result is bound to be destructive. We have found that frequently on our rivers, streams and lakes. Where there is over-fishing in any of these the time will come when nature will not be able to keep up the supply, and there is great difficulty in supplementing the loss by restocking. The time to lock the stable is before the steed is stolen, and the time to protect our fisheries is now. True there is at present very little danger from steam trawling, and I hope there will be very little danger so far as depletion goes on this side of the Atlantic. Our natural conditions are different and, as pointed out bv Mr. Cowie, the season on this side in which this steam trawling can be carried on, is comparatively short and there is time for nature to replenish herself. Still there is danger, and the question is what is the remedy. Some argue this method of fishing should be absolutely forbidden. The Dominion government has power to prohibit any Canadian engaging in it. That may be very true, but will that' help out the situation? There are some 30 or 40 French trawlers operating off the Grand Banks and a couple of trawlers operating in the United States. Are you going to deny to Canadians the rights which other people enjoy? If the passing of legislation forbidding Canadians from engaging in the business could prevent steam trawling altogether, that would be satisfactory, but it would be very ineffective when other countries are allowed to engage in this business. It is argued that the evil can be prevented by prohibiting the landing in Canada of fish caught in trawlers. That is a pretty strong argument, but I do not know how it would work out when practically tested. It would certainly lead to great complications with other countries. It might lead to reprisals on the part of these other countries, and I fear might not he productive of the good result desired. The only effect such prohibition would have would be that the fish would be landed, say in St. Pierre or Newfoundland or the United States, and the trawling would go on just the same. Of course the fishermen on the

Canadian side would not see the fish landing and that might relieve their minds to some extent, but the trawling would go on just the same. To forbid Canadians from engaging in that business while others were allowed the right would be of no effect. The same thing was tried in the old country. The Moray Firth was there closed to British trawlers, but the result was that in a short time the English ships went to Norway, floated the Norwegian flag, and came to the Moray Firth, fished outside the three mile limit and landed their fish, so that the only persons affected were the Scotch trawlers. The evil of trawling went on just the same. Prevent our Canadians from trawling and they will do what was done in the Moray Firth cases. They will register their trawlers in some foreign port and then fish with impunity outside the three-mile limit. So the evil cannot be remedied by prohibiting our own citizens from engaging in the business.
As regards forbiding the landing of Canadian fish caught in Canadian waters, I do not think, as I said before, that remedy would be very effective. Notwithstanding the strong feeling in the old country at present against trawling, they have not gone so far as to say that fish caught by steam trawling shall not be permitted to be landed. In 1908, the British parliament passed legislation entitled, ' The Prohibited Areas Extension Act '. Section 1 of that Act provides:
From and after the passing of this Act it shall not be lawful to sell or land in the United Kingdom any fish caught by the method of fishing known as steam trawling, or other trawling within the areas in which such methods of fishing are prohibited by the Herring Fishery (Scotland) Act, 1889, and by laws made thereunder.
It will be observed that this Act did not prohibit the landing of fish caught by steam trawlers generally, but only fish caught in these prohibited waters, the idea being to conserve these prohibited waters. But they did not deem it wise to pass such legislation as would totally prohibit the landing of fish caught in trawlers, and I do not know that it would be opportune or *wise to pass such legislation here.
What then is the remedy? The order in council of the 9th of Steptember, 1908, prohibits fishing by means of trawling within the three-mile limit, and in the bays and harbours of Canada, but unfortunately that does not help our inshore fisheries. Off the shores our fishermen set their trawls from two to six miles, ibut as soon as .a steam trawler appears, off the coast our local fishermen are obliged to withdraw their trawls because they do not want to take any chances of 'having their gear worth a couple of hundred dollars or more, destroyed. True, there are not many
instances of a steam trawler destroying the hook and line trawl, but the reason 13 that the local fishermen take the precaution of not setting these when the steam trawler is at work. They are, however, prevented from pursuing their honourable avocation, and I say a great hardship and injustice is done to them.
'The remedy suggested by my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) seems to be one that will go very far towards alleviating the situation so far as the shore fishermen are concerned. They are a body of men far too important to be treated with indifference and are well worthy of the eulogies paid them by my hon. friend. They have a right to exist just as well as the steam trawler.
While the shore fishermen have no objection to the trawlers prosecuting their industry, if it is carried on in such a way that there is no danger of destroying the inshore fishermen's gear or injuring the fisheries generally, at the same time, they ask, and ask reasonably, that they also should be allowed to live. This is a case of live and let live. They do not object to the steam trawler offering to take fish to be supplied fresh to the Montrealmarket, at all seasons of the year, which is the argument put forward by the Maritime Fish Corporation, the owners of the 'Wren,' yet they say :	Let us live also. A
regulation ought to be passed whereby the shore fishermen can carry on his avocation, the avocation of his fathers, an honest and honourable one, while the steam trawler carries on its work if it wants to and provided there is no danger of permanent injury to the fisheries by the trawlers doing so. That, of course, as pointed out by the hon. member for Guysborough can only be accomplished by international regulations. And there is every reason to hope that this state of things will be brought about. Trawling is not popular. It is not popular in the old country, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Guysborough. Not only Great Britain,, but the continental countries as well, are passing severe legislation against it. In the United States it is equally unpopular. It can easily be shown that it involves danger to the fisheries of the country. I have every hope therefore that the other nations would join Canada in an effort to pass regulations to restrict the operations of the trawler. I understand there is an agitation on this subject in Newfoundland and that the government there has taken up the matter. So, it -would appear quite feasible to bring about international regulations respecting the manner of conducting this industry. There is a precedent for it. In 1839, there was a convention between France and Great Britain and that convention passed regulations for

the control of the fisheries. It is true, we have no jurisdiction beyond the three-mile limit, but there is no reason why the several nations interested should not make an international arrangement, by which the deep-sea fisheries could he preserved and the local fishermen protected. This convention of 1839 defines territorial waters as being within the three-mile limit. But it made regulations regarding the conduct of the fisheries. It permitted trawl fishing within the limits of the tw7o countries. It forbade trawl fishing in certain waters, while herring and mackerel fishing are going on. It provided that trawlers should keep three miles away from boats engaged in fishing with drift nets for herring or mackerel, and went so far as to provide that where trawling was going on, and herring or mackerel boats commenced fishing there, the trawlers should leave and get away three miles from them. Now, if some such regulations could be adopted by this country, the evils complained of by our shore fishermen would at once to a very large extent vanish. And surely, it is not too much to ask that the steam trawler should keep far enough away from the shore fishermen to enable the shore fishermen to carry on their work without danger of their gear being destroyed.
The fisheries of our shores, as the hon. member for Guysborough pointed out, are the richest in the world. The steam trawlers of the old country have to drag the net for a period of four or five hours, but on our shore they can only drag it, I understand, for 45 minutes,-Dr. Oowie says one hour, but I believe that 45 minutes is really the time before it is filled and has to be hauled up. That shows how much richer the Canadian fisheries are than the fisheries of the old country We have a heritage in our fisheries which we should make every effort to conserve and we have in. our fishermen as fine a class of men as can be found anywhere. A class of men who are deserving of the best attention of the government. And I have every confidence that the government will endeavour to have international regulations adopted that will preserve the shore fishery. For, as I have already said, this government has shown every sympathy with the shore fishermen. When an application was made by several firms in Scotland for assistance to carry on this industry of steam trawling, that assistance was promptly refused, because the government believed that the effect on this industry -was to devastate the industry. Later on, the board of trade of Halifax asked that assistance be given to the trawler that was to come out from the old country, sent by the Ross Trawling Company. I read before six o'clock the letter from the late Minister of Marine and Fisheries Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonish).
to Mr. Mitchell, in which the government promptly refused to render assistance. ,1 have had to do with the department since 1908 in connection with this trawling. For,, as I said before six o'clock the ' Wren ' has been operating every season for the past three years off the shore of Antigonish, and I have heard many complaints on the part of the fishermen and have had many remonstrances from them, to make to. the government. I have invariably found the Department of Marine and Fisheries at all times desirous of seeing that the order in council, the law prohibiting trawling within the three-mile limit should be enforced. In 1908 it was represented to jne that the trawler was operating within rthe three-mile limit. I wired to the department, and promptly there was a telegram sent to the commander of the government steamer ' Petrel ' at Georgetown, as follows:
Ottawa, October 12, 1908.
C. G. S. ' Petrel,' Georgetown, P.E.I.
You are to watch the imported trawler ' Wren ' and to see that she does not infringe the law against in-trawling within the three-mile limit. Report all possible information for the benefit of the department. You will remain in commission until further orders. Acknowledge.
C. E. KINGSMILL, Rear Admiral.
Later, in 1909, it was again alleged that the trawler was operating within the three-mile limit. It is all very well to say we have an order forbidding trawlers operating within three miles of the shore, and that anybody can enforce the law, but the difficulty is, in proving the case. But let me say right here the only effective way of guarding against encroachment is to have a government cruiser constantly on the watch of the trawlers. Prevention is better than cure in such cases. The fishermen along our shore were persistent in maintaining that the trawler was operating within the three-mile limit. From what I could gather I believe that this was the fact. A prosecution wras instituted against the Captain of the ' Wren ', and he was convicted of violation of the law and was put in jail. That goes to show the disposition of the department. On the 23rd of September, 1909, I wrote to the Minister of M&rine and Fisheries calling his attention to the fact that it was alleged that the trawler ' Wren ' was operating within the three-mile limit. On 28th September, Rear Admiral Kingsmill wired the captain of the ' Constance ' to proceed to the Antigonish shore, and on the 8th of October, 1909, he writes confirming his telegram and adds:
You are therefore to keep as close a watch as possible upon her movements and do this in an unnoticeable way and with as little publicity as possible.

And last year complaint was made by the [DOT]fishermen. And, I find here, among the papers brought down a letter dated August 25, 1910, from the Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries, Mr. Johnstone, to the deputy minister of the naval service:
This department would therefore be exceedingly obliged if you would be good enough to arrange to have the fisheries protection cruiser on that portion of the coast carefully follow the operations of the ' Wren J and see that no invasion of the law is permitted by her.
It has been alleged in certain quarters that the government has been encouraging and subsidizing trawlers. I read these letters to show how unfair that charge is. Instead of assisting them, the department has shown every possible desire to protect the interests of the fishermen. They have exhausted their jurisdiction to the extent of prohibiting by order in council, this method of fishing in our territorial waters over which alone we have jurisdiction, and 1 feel quite confident that if any international arrangement can be brought about for the protection of the shore fishermen, it will be done.
That such international arrangement- can be brought about, I have no doubt. That the interest of the local or shore fishermen will be duly safeguarded in the making of such arrangements. I have every confidence in. It is, therefore, with very much pleasure I support the resolution of the hon. member for Guysborough.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. L. FRASER (Kings, P. E. I.).
speechtext:
I r'se mainly to give my endtrsement to the views of the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair). The importance of this question has been pretty well set out by that hon. gentleman and by the last speaker (Mr. Chisholm), of Antigonish, and I do not think that anything I can say can add much to its weight. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) and a great many of the officers of his department, I think, are pretty well alive to the importance of the maritime provinces fisheries. We hear much of the conservation of natural resources, and we wish that the fisheries, the great natural resource of the maritime provinces should also be conserved. And while I must say there is room for improvement, I trust the department will see to it that this great menace to the fishermen of the maritime provinces which has been mentioned here, the steam trawling business, now in its inception, will be dealt with at once and effectively. It is without doubt destructive, and is a serious matter to the fishermen. I have my information from the fishermen themselves, with a great many of whom I come into contact, and they unanimously express great objection to this method of fishing. They say that it is ruinous. Now, I do not know whether the
department is fully alive to the disastrous effects of this method of fishingbut from the report that was read here this evening I think they cannot be well informed. It would appear that this officer of the department who was sent down there condemned his own report, because he says he takes his information from the corporation that has been referred to. He was sent down there with certain authority to examine the question and report upon xc, but instead of doing so, he finds a judgment, and says that he takes his information from the captain, or the corporation of a certain fishing concern in Nova Scotia. Now such a report must be entirely valueless to the department. I did not catch the name of the officer. But I would ask the minister to weigh that report and if, as I understood the hon. member for Guysborough to say, this officer got his information entirely from the corporation that was engaged in the steam fishing, then the report must be valueless. But I can assure the minister that my information comes direct from the fishermen, and I know that when this method ol fishing came into operation they were alarmed, and they have been alarmed ever since, because they consider that method destructive. The hon. member for Guysborough also read a report from a British commission on these matters, which I think is conclusive as to the destructive nature of this method 'of fishing. Now there was a man whose name was mentioned here, I think it was Cowie, and if I am not mistaken he was himself engaged in the steam tra-wling business. He reports apparently that steam trawling was not destructive. His report would be of the same value as that of the corporation who reported to the official of the department.
I think Mr. Cowie was engaged in steam trawling, and if my memory serves me right, this is the same Mr. Cowie who received certain sums of money from this government for making certain investigations-the minister will correct me if I am mistaken. But according to my memory, Mr. Cowie received large sums of money for performing certain services for this government some years ago in relation to the fisheries in the maritime provinces. I would strongly urge upon the minister to take direct evidence from those engaged in the fishing, and I think he will find that this method of fishing is fraught with a great deal of harm. As to the mode of regulation I am unable to make any suggestion to the government. Another matter I would like to mention is the recent regulations made at Washington, by which American fishermen are allowed to come within the three-mile limit, or within 1,000 yards of the shore, and set cod and herring traps. As I understood the Min- # ister of Justice the other day, he said that any one, whether coming from the United

States or from any other part of the world, could come within a thousand yards of our shores and set cod or herring traps. Now if that is the case, I believe that our fisheries will suffer a great deal of harm, and our fishermen also will be injured.

The Minister of Justice explained clearly that this regulation to which my hon. friend refers has reference only to the treaty waters, to waters on the north side of the Gulf of St. Lawrence, and I think the Magdalen Islands and part of Labrador. But it has nothing whatever to do with the_ waters of the maritime provinces.

I was not quite sure about it. Then this regulation only affects the treaty coasts.
|Mr. BjRODEUR. There should be no misunderstanding in regard to so important a question. The agreement made with the United States the other day covers only the treaty coasts, namely, part of Labrador, from Mont Joly to Blanc Sablon, and the Magdalen Islands, that is to say, coasts which are part of Canada, and which were subject to the treaty of 1818. In virtue of that treaty American fishermen have the right to come and fish only in those parts of Canada. But so far as other parts of Canada are concerned, they have no right at all to come and fish in them.

Another thing is that under the new regulation, as I understand it, American fishermen can come in here and fish within the three-mile limit the same as Canadian fishermen, on paying a license of a dollar a year.
