speechtext: If my hon. friend is referring to the reciprocity arrangement, it does not touch the fishing privileges at all, it deals with the exchange of commodities. In the particular matter to which the hon. gentleman refers, the effect is that the modus vivendi which has been in operation now for some time, is continued, with the payment of a nominal fee. In the Chamberlain-Bayard treaty it was proposed that if free fish could be obtained the conditions of the modus vivendi should be granted to them free of charge. We have provided, not to grant them free, but to charge a nominal license fee of one dollar per annum.

I would urge upon the government to take into serious consideration this whole question of steam tra\Vl-ing, and to obtain their information from reliable sources. I think our fisheries deserve to be protected as well as any other of our natural resources such as timber and coal. The member for Guysborough * stated that the largest number of steam trawlers on the coast was twenty. Since then I think the number has been inereas-Mr. FRASER.
ing, and the situation now demands the immediate attention of the government.
Are you prophesying for yourself?

No, but I can prophesy for the hon. gentleman, because of the speech which he made to-night. I need not fear the fishermen very much. Now, the hon. gentleman said that the government passed a minute of council. He had very great sympathy with the government, but
he did not seem to have very much sympathy for the fishermen. If he can get the government out of trouble the poor fishermen may look out for themselves. He did not seem to care anything about the fishermen. But he said that they had passed an order in council forbidding beam trawling. What else did they do? They permitted trawling up and down the straits anywhere provided it was outside the three-mile limit. But the hon. gentleman knows that they could not operate their trawls four or five miles out without interfering with the shore fisheries of Antigonish or Guysborough. Does not this hon. gentleman know that these fishermen fish outside of the three-mile limit, and that' it is there that they find their best fishing grounds? Sometimes the fish come close into the shore, and at other times they are outside of the three-mile limit. These steam trawlers may go up and down the coast and destroy the shore fisheries. My hon. friend read a lot from reviews and quoted a lot of resolutions passed by everybody but the people of Canada, but the people of the maritime provinces, whose opinions he should have presented to the House. I challenge him here to-night, I defy him to contradict the statement, as I challenge the hon. member for Guysborough, that there is not a fisherman in the maritime provinces who is not against this. They are unanimous, not a single fisherman favours it, and I challenge either of these gentlemen to get up and say that I am mistaken in that view.
Who says to the contrary?

The hon. gentleman dare not say to the contrary, but he argues very much against that view, as I will be able to show. That being the case, was it not up to this government, in the interest of the people engaged in the fishing industry, that there should be no such thing as a steam traivler permitted in the maritime provinces? Was it not up to this government not to pass this minute of council, not to allow them to fish outside of the three-mile limit, but to prevent them from fishing in Canada at all? If they had done that would they not have saved the fishermen of the maritime provinces? The hon. member for Antigonish and the hon. member for Guysborough know something about the men who control this steam trawler * Wren.'
No.

No, you are mistaken.
Mr. CROSBY'. Never mind, then; we will let that go for what it is worth.
It would be interesting to know who control the ' Wren.'
I know that the Whitmans who support my hon. friend very strongly are the most interested, they buy the fish.
I confess I did not know that.

I am quite satisfied my hon. friend knows very little. I know that the Whitmans who are great supporters of my hon. friend buy the fish, whether they are interested in the steamer or not. My hon. friend from Antigonish seemed to have an idea that there was a scarcity of fish and indicated that it was necessary to have steam trawlers to supply that deficiency. I would ask any hoh. member if with fish, netting the fishermen from one half cent to two cents per pound, there is anything in the cost of fish that would necessitate new methods of catching them?
I do not think that any fisherman in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, or Quebec will say there was ftny necessity for steam trawlers because we have to pay too much for our fish. The hon. members who have spoken must admit that the introduction of steam trawlers would destroy the livelihood of the fishermen of the maritime provinces. They would destroy an industry carried on by a class of men as brave as any in Canada, These men, in order to gain a livelihood, take greater risks than men in any other industry in the world unless perhaps the mining industry.
Hon. members have given at great length statistics relating to fishing in England, Ireland, Scotland and Norway, but we are here to govern our own people, to govern Canadians, and if we can do that well we are discharging our duty because these are the people most interested. The hon. members did not give us anything that was stated by the fishermen of Antigonish or Guysborough, you would think there was no one there to speak to them. The fishermen of our maritime provinces are unanimous in believing that no steam trawlers should be allowed. Therefore, I think these hon. nrembers should make some special effort to satisfy, and do justice to these men. The only way you can do justice to them is iby a minute of council or by a vote of this parliament preventing the use of any steam trawler in the maritime provinces.
As to the preservation of the fisheries on the Great Banks we have a splendid class of men who perhaps do greater fishing on these banks than any other class. \Ve want them to be protected, and of course, it would be impossible for us to pass any legislation here that would be effective without concurrent legislation of other nations interested, particularly the United States and France, except in the ways proposed by the hon. member for Guysborough. ' Mr. SINCLAIR.
But the bon. member for Guysborough might go further and make his resolution, prevent the purchase of fish caught bysteam trawlers whether inside or outside the three-mile limit. We know as a matter of fact, all the fishermen in the maritime provinces know, that these fish are caught within the three-mile limit. My hon. friend can talk about a telegram from this admiral to the next one, but it is only waste of money, and we have to pay the bills ; the steam trawler goes on and brings the fish in just the same. [DOT]
A word with reference to the fishing industry of the maritime provinces. On the coast of Nova Scotia our fishermen fish the whole winter through without any protection whatever. I would suggest to the Minister of Marine -arid Fisheries that he should have a few of the ships under control of his department parole the Bay of Fundy and the coast of Nova Scotia, in order to succour fishing vessels that may be overtaken -by sudden gales. In the United States during the last few years they have employed their revenue cutters in patrolling the coasts in this way. This year they have had ten patrolling the coast from Cape Hatteras north. They published statistics last year showing that these vessels -had saved hundreds of lives and millions of dollars worth of property. I can see no reason why the Minister of Marine and Fisheries should not have some of his steamers patrolling east from Halifax and others west from Halifax, particularly in stormy weather so that there may be some encouragement to the fishermen, and some hope that they may he brought safely to shore in case they are overtaken by storm. I am -quite in accord with the resolution moved by the hon. member for Guysborough, and with all that -he has said in supporting it, Nothing can he said to augment his argument. My only objection to the resolution is that it does not go far enough, and I would appeal to the hon. member for Guysborough and to the hon. member for Antigonish to use all their influence to induce the government to stop the sale in Canada of fish caught by steam trawlers. Then we shall have what our fishermen desire -and must h-ave if they are to have justice.

speechtext: In justice to the hon. member for Guysborough, I feel it my duty to state that he communicated to me on Saturday that he intended to bring this resolution up; so that if there is any fault it is my own.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to offer a few observations on the subject before the House, which is one of unlimited importance to the maritime provinces and to Canada as a whole. I take a great interest in this * subject, and that interest is intensified

by the fact that 40 per cent of the people of the county which I have the honour to represent are directly or indirectly interested in fishing. I therefore desire to call the attention of the House to the importance of the industry to this country. We find that the number of men engaged in the fishing industry in Canada is something like 69,000, that the value of the fish and fish products of last year in Canada was in the vicinity of $30,000,000, and that about $17,000,000 of capital is invested in the industry. These figures show the very great importance of the fishing industry in Canada, and therefore, it is the duty of every member of this House to do what he can to preserve that industry in every respect. I understood the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Crosby), to find fault with the government for not having done more to prevent the operation of beam trawlers within the three-mile limit. As I understand, the government passed an order in council in 1908 prohibiting .the use of the beam trawl within the three-mile limit, and in doing this, they exhausted their jurisdiction. I think it is conceded by members on both sides of this House, that they could not do more than that. The hon. gentleman says that beam trawlers have not been prevented from operating within the three-mile limit. I may say that I have had some experience in that regard. I -was notified by the fishermen that beam trawlers were operating off the coast of Inverness. I at once telegraphed to the department, and in reply to my request one of the boats of the Government Protective Service was sent there and could very quickly redressed that grievance had they followed up those trawlers in their operations. I am informed they did not do this as they might. With regard to the effect of the operation of steam trawlers on our fishing grounds, from all the information I can gather, it is destined to have the most destructive consequences so far as our fisheries are concerned. To show the great interest that is taken in this subject in the province of Nova Scotia, I may state that the local government of Nova Scotia then passed a resolution in April, 1908, asking this government to use all its power to prevent these trawlers from operating around the coast of that province; and every fishermen's union and several maritime councils in the province passed resolutions to the same effect. This shows the great interest taken in the question by the people of Nova Scotia generally. The operation of the beam trawler is particularly injurious to the inshore fishermen. These men, who engage in hand-line fishing, trawl fishing and net fishing, set their gear anywhere from three to ten miles from the shore. We can imagine long lines of trawls set along the shore, nets of varying lengths set at various distances from
the shore, and lobster traps set three or four miles from the shore would fare when in the course of beam trawlers in operation. Even if the beam trawler never comes within the three-mile limit, a large portion of this gear extends beyond that limit, and when the beam trawler sets out shortly before dark and steams along these fishing grounds, we can imagine the result. It would be the same as it has been in the old country. The inevitable result is the destruction of all the fishermen's gear set in the ground where the beam trawler operates. It is in anticipation of this destruction that the fishermen suffer most. When they know that a beam trawler is going to visit their fishing grounds, they are obliged to remove their gear to the shore. This means that their avocation, at least for the time, is gone. They are thus discouraged and will in many cases abandon fishing for^ all time. I have had strong representations on this subject from the fishermen of my own county. I do not intend to heap any encomiums on the fishermen as was done by other speakers to-night. It is not necessary to do so. The world knows their many deeds of bravery, their trials and hardships. If I did, I might be charged with throwing boquets at them in anticipation of something that may occur within the next couple of years. I may say, however, that I was met by a delegation of fishermen from along the coast of Inverness a few days before I came to this House, after Christmas, and they represented to me that the conditions there were such that if the beam trawler is allowed to continue to operate along that coast, the 40 per cent of our people who are dependent on fishing must turn to something else to eke out a livelihood. With regard to the effect of the beam trawler upon the feeding grounds and the spawning ground, I know that there are reports on file to the effect that thev cannot cause very great evils in this respect, but I attach a great deal of importance to the opinions of the fishjrmen, I have great confidence in their powers of observation, because they are people who devote their whole time to the fishing industry, .which to them is their only means of livelihood, and consequently they cannot fail, possessing as they, do at least an average amount of intelligence, to have the most accurate knowledge regarding the fishing and spawning grounds I am bound then to accept the honest representations of these people. When I tell you that these engines of destruction are capable of gathering even the large anchors of ships, as they have done in the last year, (and carried them to the port of North Sydney), you can imagine how the bottom over which these monsters operate must be tom up. Assuming for a moment that this takes place and I think there is no doubt about it.

what must we conclude? We cannot come to any other conclusion than that the ground travelled over by these engines must be so disturbed that the fish will no longer be found there. That at any rate is the opinion of the fishermen, and I am bound to respect their views, as the views of men who have watched the movements of the fish in such cases, and I am bound to accept their opinions on .questions of nature. It may be said that a large number of steam trawlers have operated in the North Sea for a great number of years without any noticeable depletion taking place there; but, as the hon. member vfor Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) pointed out a little while .ago, in order to keep up the average supply of fish it was necessary for these trawlers to go away down to the coast of Africa, and as far north as the ice will allow them to operate. It was only by these means that they could keep up the average supply of fish. They operated, not only in the North sea, but practically from the Arctic to the southern coast of Africa.	I have pointed out
that the result of the operation of these steam trawlers is to root up and harrow the bottom. In reply we are told that where this is done by a large number of trawlers, there has been no depletion. Well, we cannot compare our small fishing grounds with those large areas in the old country but from the Arctic to the coast of Africa. Take 15 or 20 trawlers' and operate them on one of those banks on our coasts and imagine them travelling over these banks four or five months in the year, it will not take them long to cover quite an area, in fact a large fraction of our small inshore boats will be gone over, and you may take it for granted that the area they cover is going to be destroyed for quite a while. That is the opinion of fishermen, and I will accept that opinion against the reports of any scientist or anybody else with regard to this phase of the question.
Let me refer now to the destruction of small fish. We are told by one of the officers sent down to our coast that there is absolutely no destruction of the small fish by beam trawling. But this officer, Mr. Halkett, I understand, made only one visit to the fishing grounds. It is known to men who know anything at all about fishing, that there are certain sections of fishing grounds frequented by the large fish and certain other sections frequented by the small fish. Would it be a very great stretch of the imagination to think that the owner of one of these boats would steer clear of the ground generally frequented by small fish, and go to those grounds where large fish were generally found, and thus give this government inspector the opportunity to say that no small fish were destroyed. In any event I do not see that Mr. Halkett could have obtained a very thorough grasp Mr. CHISHOLM (Inverness).
of his subject by merely going out on one trip, and then making his report.- I have often gone out in a fishing boat myself, and I invariably found that a considerable fraction of the boats' catch was small unmarketable fish. This being the case, surely it is not reasonable to suppose that beam trawlers do not catch quantities of this kind of fish when they are found by all other means of fishing. When on this question of small fish, let me say that I do not see why we should not have a reasonable proportion of small fish just as they have in the old country. But the trouble is we have not any statistics to show what proportion of small fish are caught whereas in the old country they have.- In the evidence given by Mr. G. L. Alwaxt before the committee on the fishery investigation appointed by the British government in 1907, to look into this question of steam trawlers, he said that in January, 1902, 19,230 cwt., of immature fish were brought into the port of Grimsby; in March, following 23,770 cwt., were brought into the same port; in April, 34,000 cwt., and in May, 32,000 cwt., or in all 109,000 cwt., brought into Grimsby in these four months. It is most unreasonable to suppose that we in Canada do not have at least .a reasonable proportion of small fish, and if we have the same proportion as in the old country, we can easily see the destruction wrought by steam trawling.
I have just a word or two to say with regard to the operations of steam trawlers within the three-mile limit. I am of the opinion that the steam trawlers do operate within that limit. On more occasions than one that famous beam trawler the ' Wren,' and another whose name I do not remember, operated off the coast of Inverness last year. This steam trawler would come about dark, move along aimlessly, and just as soon as night fell would drop their nets, and steam on. That I have from the fishermen of Inverness, who have watched their movements. From their statements I am satisfied that their steam trawler did operate within the three-mile limit. I have strong representation from the fishermen asking the government to send one of their cruisers down there to follow the operations of this steam trawler. That is what the fishermen want more than anything else. They recognize that this government has exhausted its jurisdiction so far as preventing the operations of steam trawlers is concerned, and what they ask the government to do now is to send down one of their cruisers to prevent that steam trawler from operating within the three-mile limit.
As far as the area outside the three-mile limit is concerned, I am in accord with the hon. gentleman who preceded me. The only remedy we can hope for is of an international character. I am satisfied there are

no other means we can use, and I am in great hopes that international regulations can be secured and that soon. As I have on several occasions said, the fishing industry ox Canada depends upon some regulations of an international character by which the steam trawler will be kept away from the coast, and I trust and believe that the government-will exhaust every means within its power to have such international regulations as will for all time settle this burning question, and thus save our fishing industry fcr our own fishermen rather than for steam trawl corporations.

Mr. Speaker, as the representative of a constituency comprising within its limits a large number of fishermen, I beg leave to say a few words in support of the resolution submitted to the House by my hon. friend from Guys-borough (Mr. Sinclair).
The fishing gear and engines, to which he referred were brought to my attention within the last two years by. fishermen in my constituency, several of whom have not the means to secure them. These fishing engines are surely harmful and their use is likely to deprive fishermen of their means of livlihood. Apart from those trawlers which have just been mentioned, there are also what is called trap nets, used largely by fishermen from the United States. These people engage in the waters of the St. Lawrence provided with such immense traps, and often times prevent those fishing by hand from getting a living for themselves and their families out of these same waters.
Representations have been forthcoiping to me that I should approach the Minister of Marine and the government in this connection and voice the well grounded grievances of the people of the north shore of the St. Lawrence from Natashquan eastwards.
I am not in a position to express an opinion as to the actually mischievous nature of the fishing engines mentioned; I have no personal experience in this connection. But if any credence is to be given to the unanimous reports of the fishing community settled over a distance of five hundred miles along th.e north shore of the St. Lawrence, I think I am warranted in calling on the Minister of Marine to inquire into the question, with a view to amending the regulations in regard to licenses, in such a way that the poor man may be in a position to earn a living side by side with those in more affluent circumstances.
It is stated that fast American schooners, provided with trap nets, have been observed operating along the coast, within forty feet from shore, directly opposite the fishermen's houses. Such enormous quantities were being caught, that the boats could not hold them; nevertheless they
would throw any surplus overboard, rather than let these poor fishermen have any for charity's sake.
Considering these hardships, I deem it incumbent on me to request that the Minister of Marine should inquire through his officers as to what is going on in those parts, so as to find out some means of protecting the people living along that shore. After all they are Canadians. They are not all electors for the time being, but I trust they will be before long. They are Canadians of all origins, who have been settled in those quarters for hundreds of years and have developed a considerable trade in fish. On account of recent developments in carrying on the industry, these good people are liable to lose their only means of subsistence, as they are unable to compete with such powerful engines of destruction as those referred to. An attempt is made to justify the use of such engines on the ground of the needs of the general fish market. There is something in that; however, consumers would not feel the inconvenience of dispensing now and then with fish to the same degree as the poor fisherman would that of dispensing with bread.
Complaints are being forwarded from the maritime provinces. People in that part of the country which I represent have requested that I should voice their grievances before the government. That is what I have done. I have apprised the government of their views by means of records which I have in person laid before the Minister of Marine. If such representations are worthy of attention, regulations should be enacted at once with a view to protecting the poorer class against the richer, and especially against outsiders, mostly Newfoundlanders and Americans who come and fish in our waters, while Canadians are made to suffer therefrom. Under the circumstances the government should see to it as soon as possible, and find some means of protecting our people against outsiders, while at the same time, keeping aloof from any international entanglements.

speakeroldname: Mr. L. P. BRODEUR (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).
speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to be able to offer my congratulations to the hon. member for Guysborough for having brought to the attention of the House this important question of steam trawling in the Gulf of the St. Lawrence and on the banks of Newfoundland. This question has attracted the attention of the department ever since the first steam trawler came to our shores. It was in the month of June, 1908, if I remember well, that the first steam trawler appeared on the coast of Canada. Only a few months elapsed when the department, on representations which were made especially by my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. COMMONS
Sinclair), found it advisable to take action in the matter. I recommended to my colleagues to pass regulations prohibiting the use of steam trawlers within the three-mile limit. That regulation provides:
That His Excellency the Governor General in Council in virtue of section 54 of the Fisheries Act, chapter 45 Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, is pleased to make and does hereby make the following fishery regulation:
The use or operation of vessels known as steam trawlers, operating beam, otter or other trawls for the purpose of catching fish is prohibited within the three-mile limit and in the bays and harbours of Canada.
This regulation was immediately put into force and we have taken the necessary steps to provide that it should be absolutely observed. Some violations of the regulations did occur on the part of the steam trawler which was then operating on the coast of Canada. Instructions were immediately given to the^ commanders of our fishery protection service that the vessels of the service should follow this steam trawler in order to see that the regulations were rigidly observed. As there were vio* lations of the regulation, we took these people before the court, and, if I remember rightly the captain of the vessel was convicted and even sent to jail. That shows that the department was anxious to prevent these steam trawlers from operating in the bays on the coasts of our territory.
That shows what is the policy of the government. I may say further that the policy of the government has always been to obtain some international regulation under which these steam trawlers could be prohibited from operating to the detriment of our shore fishermen. When I was in England in 1909, I had occasion to take up this question with the imperial authorities. It was on the occasion of the Imperial Defence Conference, and Newfoundland's representative was Sir Edward Morris, the Prime Minister. Sir Edward Morris and myself discussed this question with the authorities of the Colonial Office, and we pressed on His Majesty's government the desirability of obtaining an international arrangement for the regulation of the fisheries on the banks. Our object was to obtain an international arrangement with France and the United States, because those were fire only two countries who were engaged to any extent in fishing on the great banks. At that time France already had a certain number of steam trawlers operating on the banks, and the number was increasing. According to statistics I have in my hand in 1907 there were 9 French steam trawlers on the banks, and in 1908 this number had increased to 29: so in one year there was an increase of 20 steam trawlers sent from France to fish on the great banks. I had occasion also, Mr. BRODEUR.
when in Europe, to meet some people in France who were interested in steam trawling, and I found that public opinion was divided in regard to it. In the northern part of France, by which I mean that region including the ports of Dunquerque and Boulogne, the fishermen were mostly in favour of the steam trawlers. But in the southern part of) France, south of Finis-terre, all the fishermen, if I may judge of the view's I heard expressed by a member of the Chambre des Deputes, were absolutely opposed to the steam trawlers. The other country wre had to deal with was the United States. Up to the present year, I think the United States have sent no steam trawlers on the great banks or into the Gulf of the St. Lawrence, but I am now informed that during the present year a couple of steam trawlers have been despatched from Gloucester or Boston, and more are likely to visit our banks. That shows, Mr. Speaker, that the steps which were taken by Sir Edward Morris and myself in 1909 to induce the imperial government to take up the question with these two countries, wras a step in the right direction, was a step which, if I may judge from the discussion we have had to-day, commends itself to the good opinion of both sides of the House. I may add that since then some communications of a confidential nature have been exchanged between this government and the imperial government on that question, and it is now engaging the serious consideration of the imperial government. Therefore, when mv hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) states in his resolution that steps should be taken, he is stating what has already been done by the Canadian government.	,
Now there are some objections which occur in considering the question of prohibition, or of regulation of steam trawlers outside the territorial limit. The first objection we met with was as to how far the territorial jurisdiction of Canada extended. There is no doubt that within the three-mile limit our jurisdiction is unquestioned; but outside the three-mile limit we have no jurisdiction. But how far have we- jurisdiction in the bays? You are aware that for some years the question has been agitated in Canada and in the United States as to the extent of our territorial jurisdiction in the bays. In the case of a bay only six miles wide there is no doubt about our jurisdiction; but in bays wider than that, the question arose whether foreign fishermen could come in and fish outside the three-mils limit on each side of the bay. However, that question has been settled so far as the United States is concerned, and in a way which I am sure is satisfactory to the Canadian people. The Hague award stated that certain bays were absolutely within our jurisdiction and our

territory; as respects others, a recommendation was made that some regulation should be passed not including those bays as part of Canadian territory; and as respects others also some boundaries were fixed. So this first objection which was met in discussing the question is now decided in our favour by the Hague award. It has been said that the method of steam trawling is a great improvement upon the old mode of fishing. I do not propose to discuss that question now at any length. I may say, however, that it is considered advisable that in all matters with regard to the fisheries we should adopt absolutely the same principle. For example, we have to make regulations in some cases to limit the catch of fish. Take the regulations we have passed with regard to purse seines, with regard to traps, with regard to pound nets. In many cases we have adopted regulations to prohibit the use of certain fishing methods because they were too destructive, in order to preserve our fisheries, and in order the more effectively to regulate them. We have been adopting all sorts of restrictions in order to preserve the fisheries. Take the issue of licenses, the close seasons, the size of mesh, and the gears, which I have just mentioned and which gears have been prohibited in order to prevent a too active catch of fish. Then, take steam trawling; although this is an improvement on the old system, I should say that if this improvement is still of such a nature that it could be considered as exposing our fisheries to depletion, we should take the necessary steps to prevent the use of such engines. That is what we have done in the regulation that I have just mentioned, and that is what we have done in the representations which have been made to the imperial authorities in order to bring about a conference (between the different countries interested. We have to consider three main points, first, the conservation of the fisheries; second, the interests of the fishermen, and third, the requirements of the fish trade. The conservation of the fisheries is certainly a thing which appeals to most people interested in the preservation of our natural resources generally speaking. We spend large sums of money in order to protect our natural resources, and we, at the same time, take all the necessary steps in order to preserve those natural resources. The fisheries are certainly one of the best natural resources that we have, and I think it would be a pity if all the steps necessary v ere not taken to preserve those fisheries.
Nothing too good can be said in favour of the hardy fishermen who daily expose their lives in order to get their livelihood.
very beautiful and interesting picture of the work and devotion of these men has 99
been presented by my hon. friend from G-uysborough, and I do not intend to say very much upon this point because he has done it in so excellent a way. But, I may say that we should always keep in our minds in the framing of our regulations and the making of our laws, the interests of those fishermen, and that is the reason which induced me to recommend to my colleagues, as I did in 1908, the prohibition of steam trawling, which I described a few minutes ago. I must admit that the requirements of the fisheries should equally not be lost sight of. The requirements of the fisheries are very important and it is acknowledged that the government, in framing these regulations, should also look to the preservation of that interest. In connection with that, I think it is only a matter of justice to read to the House a letter which was addressed to me by the manager of a company which owns the steam trawler the ' Wren.' This letter is dated about a month ago, and it reads as follows:
Maritime Fish Corporation, Limited,
St. Nicholas Building,
Montreal, December 12, 1910. Hon. L. P. Brodeur,
Minister of Marine and Fisheries,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-Re steam trawlers. My attention has been called to a resolution proposed by Mr. Sinclair, member for Guysborough county, Nova Scotia, which is to be brought before the House of Commons, and I have been directed by the board of directors of this company to place some information before you relating to the advantages attached to this mode of fishing, with a view to developing the fisheries of the Atlantic coast.
This company purchased from the Pioneer Steam Trawling Company in May last the steam trawler ' Wren,' and prior to the time we took over this trawler, very little had been done, and the steamer was not operated for commercial purposes.
To develop a steady and uniform supply of sea fish to the inland cities, this company decided it was absolutely necessary to improve upon the methods of fishing pursued in Guysborough county, realizing the Department of Marine and Fisheries were doing their share towards the development of this industry. P/ior to this time the fish dealers in the larger centres of Montreal and Toronto were dependent upon Portland and Boston for their supplies of fresh haddock and codfish, which was purely through lack of organization on the part of any company to give the dealers a steady supply. In previous years for many weeks the dealers were without fish, and at times had to pay exorbitant prices from the United States markets. We are glad to state that from May 1, 1910, the trade have been largely supplied with fresh fish from the Atlantic coast, taken by the steam trawlers operating out of Canso. This was owing to severe storms along the coast for several weeks in the month of September, and for one week at the latter part of September the



Canadian markets were absolutely and wholly supplied by steam trawler fish at from three and one-half to four cents per pound delivered in Montreal, whereas the quotations from Boston and Portland during the same period were seven and one-half to eight cents per pound.
Steam trawlers are being operated out of Grimsby and Aberdeen, Scotland, to a very large extent, and at the present time clubs of fishermen realizing the advantage this mode of fishing has, are now owning and operating these steamers. I inclose copy of a clipping taken from the Gloucester ' Times/ dated November 29, in which it refers to the third steam trawler of a proposed fleet of vessels launched in the United States. Since that time I am informed another steamer has been ordered, and if we in Canada are to compete with our friends on the other side of the border, we must have modern and up-to-date appliances.
Furthermore, from information I have been given, some thirty-five French steam trawlers operated last season on the Atlantic coast, and I cannot see that it is fair to propose legislation prohibiting Canadians from being on an equal footing with other nations.
To further illustrate to you the advantages afforded to fish merchants and fishermen operating along the coast, this company has paid to the fishermen one-half cent per pound more for their fresh haddock landed than in any previous year during the same. months, and the product instead of being dried or salted as it lias been in the other years, was largely disposed of in the fresh and smoked state, and the fishermen through this means have received cash for all the product offered immediately landed, whereas in other years where they were dependent upon foreign markets, the product has been held awaiting favourable market conditions.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) ALFRED H. BRITTAIN, Director and General Sales Manager.
This letter is certainly of some importance and I thought that for the benefit of the discussion, I should read it to the House. Of course, I do not agree with everything that is included in it because 1 think that we could very easily get a supply of fish at all times. Of course, we must give some consideration to the representations which are made in that letter. My correspondent has alluded to what the department has been doing in order to encourage the sale of fresh fish on the markets of Ontario and Quebec. We thought that it was a very serious handicap for our fish trade that in former years the markets of Montreal and Toronto were almost entirely supplied with fish coming from the United States.
The information I had, however, was that while this fish was virtually caught in Canadian waters, most of the business on the coast was carried on by American fishermen, who were taking our fish to the American markets, Gloucester and Boston, and from there were distributing it to dif-Mr. BRODEUR.
ferent parts of th.e United States and Canada; and it is a remarkable thing that during many years we were obliged to pay duty on our own fish, that is to say, fish caught in Canadian waters, transported to Boston and Gloucester, and then shipped from there to the Canadian markets of Montreal and Toronto. It was thought that some steps should be taken to put an end to this state of affairs. My colleagues appropriated a certain sum of money which was devoted to facilitating the transportation of fresh fish from the maritime provinces, or from the Pacific coast to the interior of Canada. I am glad to he able to state that this policy has produced very good results. I find that in 1906 there were imported into Ontario and Quebec from the United States 1,968,572 pounds of fish. In 1908 this amount was reduced to 1,180,543 pounds, and in 1910, in the last fiscal year, the amount imported was only 751,569. That shows that in spite of the increase in our population, in spite of our large consumption of fish, because the consumption has increased largely in the last few years, there has been a large reduction in imports. Why? Because we have paid to the express companies and the railway companies a part of the cost of transportation of fresh fish in cold storage and paid one-third of the cost of the transportation of fresh fish by express. Now, all the fish which is consumed in Montreal, Toronto and Ottawa, in fact in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, comes from the Atlantic provinces of Canada, being transported in the way I have just described. This policy has been very beneficial, and I hone that within a short time it will not be necessary for the government to continue to subsidize the transportation of fresh fish, because people will have become accustomed to eating fish and to receiving it direct from the maritime provinces. This shows the result of the policy adopted by the government. I do not believe that this result is due to the use of steam trawlers, but simply to the improved facilities which have been given for the transportation of fresh fish.	,
How shall this question of international agreement be considered? Perhaps it would be advisable for me to refer for a minute or two to the arrangements or agreements which exist in Europe upon that question. Since 1839 there has been an agreement between France and England as to the fisheries on a certain section of the Channel waters bordering those two countries. This agreement provided for the regulation of the length of beam, and the size of the mesh, and prevented anv trawler fishing near a herring or net fishing boat in such a way that the objection made to-day to the use of steam trawlers on the ground that, thev were destroying the fishing gear of herring fishermen or fishermen using

set trawls, are entirely overcome. The regulations under the agreement are framed in such a way that it is absolutely impossible for any steam trawler to interfere in any way with the ordinary fisherman, and to destroy his gear. In 1882 the North Sea Convention was made. To this convention Great Britain. Germany, Holland, France, Belgium, Denmark, Norway and Sweden were parties. This agreement defines, first, what are territorial waters, adopting the head line theory for which we have fought so many years with the United States, and which was at last recognized by the award of The Hague tribunal. It states, also, that within such territorial waters no boat can fish except with the authority of the country adjoining these waters. It also provides that the trawl fishermen are not permitted near drift net or long line fishermen, and even that when fishermen come to fish with nets the steam trawlers must leave the bank and go and fish elsewhere. This was the agreement embodied in the North sea convention, which certainly should form the basis of any agreement which may be reached between Great Britain, the United States and France. Under this North Sea Convention and in virtue of the powers which England possessed, laws were passed in 1885 empowering the Board of Fisheries of Scotland to prohibit the use of steam trawls in territorial waters; to-day, with the exception of one place, steam trawling is absolutely prohibited in the territorial waters of Scotland. Later a regulation was passed prohibiting the landing in Scotland of fish caught by steam trawlers. But, unfortunately, and I call the attention of my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Crosby) to this point, instead of helping to preserve the fisheries, this regulation has worked detrimentally to the interests of the other fishermen. In fact, the foreign fishermen who took their fish outside of the three-mile limit were prevented from landing them at anv Port in Scotland, and they had to go to Grimsby or some other port in England where the regulations did not apply.
The hon. member for Halifax suggested that we might have some law or regulation prohibiting the landing in Canada of fish caught by steam trawlers. I am afraid that such a regulation would work detrimentally to our own fishermen. At present they have the advantage of sending fish from the maritime provinces to the inland cities of Canada ; but the effect of prohibiting the landing of fish caught by steam trawlers, especially at seasons when they could not be caught by the other fishermen, would be that the New England fishermen would catch the fish off our coasts, carry it to the United States, and then sell it to us as American fish, and we would have to pay the duty on it. The Americans would 99i	*
have all the benefit of that situation to the detriment of our own fishermen. Therefore, I think we had better try to reach an agreement with the United States and with France upon some such regulation as that which exists in Europe by virtue of the North Sea Convention. If the total prohibition of steam trawlers could be agreed upon by these countries, it would be the best thing that could happen to us. But if it should be impossible to reach such an agreement, I think the next best thing for us would be to try to get an agreement such as I have just mentioned.
My hon. friend from Guysborough and other speakers have referred to the report made by Mr. Halkett, the naturalist of the department. Perhaps it is only just to Mr. Halkett, who is certainly a very good officer, in whom I have always had full confidence, that I should read" his report. It is not a definite report, but only a summary of his observations. He is going to prepare a report, which will give concisely and precisely all his observations in connection with his trip on the ' Wren.' Unfortunately, Mr. Halkett has not been well for some time, he is now absent on sick leave, and his complete report has not yet been prepared. But as soon as he returns, he will be asked to prepare that report, and I shall be glad to bring it down with the other papers. In his summary report, he says :
Having carefully followed the fishing operations carried on by steam trawlers on board the trawler 'Wren/ I have to report that the complaints made against such operations are entirely without just reason. On the contrary, instead of being exceedingly destructive and wasteful, practically everything drawn up in the great net, excepting the dogfish which are entangled in considerable numbers, is utilized and turned to account, and the very destruction of the dogfish is a benefit, whilst the men are entitled to save their livers on their own behalf. I understand that until recently the flat fishes, such as the rough-dab, were thrown away; but since the establishment of the glue factory at Canso such are now sold to that institution. There is really nothing drawn up in the net which any economical fishing corporation would ever think of wasting, and cer-tainlv the captain of the 'Wren' is awake to the interests of the Maritime Fish Corporation in this respect. The bulk of the fish caught is haddock, and it is for them that the trawling is carried on. The weight of the catch of haddock was 27,580 pounds, exclusive of 3,300 pounds of assorted small ones. This numerically, judging by the respective sizes, approximately represents some 6,895 and 1,650 fish. The weight of flat fishes was 325 pounds, of the cod 150 pounds, and of the hake 1,550 pounds, or numerically 100 flat fishes, 25 cod and 100 hake. True, I was dependent on the corporation for these figures after landing at Canso; but based on my own observations on hoard the 'Wren,' I can vouch for the figures being approximately correct. The total weight of these was 32.905 pounds, and (he number approximately 8,770. Besides leav-

ing out the dogfish there were a few silver hake, pollock, skate and gaspereau and a shad, and angler and an eel. It is difficult to form an estimate of the number of dogfish caught, but the number was very-considerable. Sometimes there would be only two or three, and at other times the net seemed to have swept through a regular school of them; their livers are out out and they are immediately destroyed and thrown overboard. Besides the true fishes there were a very limited number of squid, saved and other odds and ends like the angler, skates, &c., for making glue; and there were hardly any other invertebrates except a few worthless star fishes, &c. I will work the matter all out in a more detailed way later, but meanwhile give some broad outlines in a summary way. Occasionally, but very rarely, I saw an insignificant gaspereau or other very small fish thrown overboard, but there is virtually no waste whatsoever. The operations were carried on not closer to the land than four miles, and besides the 'Coquette' no other fishing craft was to be seen.
(Sgd.) ANDREW HALKETT,
Naturalist, Dept. Marine and Fisheries. St. John, N.B., Oct. 29, 1910.
This report, as we see, was sent direct from the maritime provinces, and I think that before condemning it, we had better wait until we have Mr. Halkett's full report, which no doubt will give the reasons for these figures, and the circumstances w'hich attended his visit on the ' Wren.' It is urged that the department should make some further experiments of the same kind in order to corroborate this report of Mr. Halkett. I am glad to accept the suggestion, and I shall he glad to give instructions to Mr. Halkett or to some other officer of the department to make further observations on the subject.

I read this merely to show that this subject has been a very live one for a considerable time. As far back as 1909 representations had been made from different sections of the province of Nova Scotia urging that steps should be taken to combat this danger as a menace to the fisheries, and on the occasion referred to, these representations found expression in the resolution I have just read.
Now, the damage which these beam trawls do, consists not only, as I have said, in destroying the spawning ground by tearing up the bottom, but also in ^he injury done to the fishermen who use what are known as trawls, consisting of long lines of fishing gear, to which at intervals shorter lines are fastened. These trawls are quite expensive, arid have to be kept in suitable condition for operation. Anything which tangles or breaks them involves considerable loss to the fishermen in straightening out the trawl and repairing it. This means loss of fishing, and consequent loss of profit to the fishermen. The subject is one which calls for prompt and vigorous action on the part of the government, as a result of this steam trawling, an intolerable condition has developed in certain waters in and about the maritime provinces. I am informed that recently one of these trawlers has entered the Bay of Fundy, and has been, or is about to prosecute its operations there. I am confident that the people who have been fishing in the Bay of Fundy will be very much opposed to this invasion, I cannot urge too strongly on the department the necessity of early and energetic steps to cope with this threatened evil. Now the department has known of this condition for some time, and we cannot help asking ourselves what the department has been doing. It seems that as far back as 1909, from the statement of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries this evening, this matter came under his personal observation, and he went so far as to discuss it with the Prime Minister of Newfoundland at the imperial conference in 1909. But thereafter, apparently, nothing has bqen done, the matter has been allowed to drift. To-day we find ourselves actually in the same condition as we were in 1908, so far as regards any steps taken by the department, I may say that I observe in the report of the department for the year 1908-9 some reference to the subject of steam trawling. There is a casual reference on Mr. JAMESON.
the part of the deputy minister in his report to the minister, appearing at page XXI, where he says:
The invasion of steam trawling off Canadian shores has been introduced this season, 1908-9, by an imported trawler named the 'Wren,' which vessel was brought to this country by a Halifax company.
Immediately urgent representations were made to the department on behalf of the shore fishermen strongly remonstrating against the operations of the vessel, the objections advanced being that large quantities of small unmarketable fish were taken and wasted, and that she was destructive to the gear of the hand liner, as well as of the grounds resorted to by them for fishing purposes.
So serious were the complaints against steam trawling immediately following its introduction, that the department procured an oiMer in council dated September 9, 1908, a copy of which is quoted. Then follows the order in council which reads:
His Excellency the Governor in Council, in virtue of the provisions of section 54 of the Fisheries Act, chapter 45, of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, is pleased to make, and doth hereby make the following fishery regulation:
The use or operation of vessels known as steam trawlers operating beam, otter or other trawls for the purpose of catching fish, is prohibited within the three-mile limit and in the bays and harbours of Canada.
The report then goes on to say:
The action of the department in procuring the order in council which prohibited this method of fishing within the three-mile limit and the bays and harbours of Canada did away with any question of encroachment on the territorial waters.
Now although this statement was made in the report of the Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries, we learn from the member for Inverness (Mr. Chisholm), tonight, that such had not been the case, that even within the three-mile limit, these trawlers are still at times prosecuting their work, and that serious injury to the fishing interests had resulted^there-from. But the main thing which we note here is that as far back as 1908, the government had actual knowledge of the conditions existing in this respect, and apparently knew that some steps were necessary in order to mitigate injury or to prevent damage, and they took the course which has been stated in the report I have read. But in the same volume, issued by the minister for the year 1908-9, we find another interesting report, which was evidently considered of sufficient importance to take a place in the volume. This report is made by John J. Cowie, an officer, if not an adviser, of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, as appendix No. 20, page 373, in the report of the minister. On page 384 he makes a

statement which I will read to the House, because taken in conjunction with the action of the department and with the statement of the deputy minister, it seems a little startling, not to say inconsistent. He says:
With regard to the framing of laws for the restriction and regulation of beam and otter trawling in Canadian waters, I luay he allowed to say that, in my opinion, all that is really necessary is the keeping of trawlers outside the three-mile limit along the coast, and outside of the ten-mile limit in hays, with rules providing that no trawler shall fish within at least three miles of any boat or vessel which is in the act of fishing for herring or mackerel, or within three miles of any vessel anchored for the purpose of line fishing, so that line fishermen shall not live in constant fear of having their fishing gear swept away and destroyed.
Those rules, dealing with extra territorial waters, would, of course, have to be mutually agreed to by the countries interested to be of any use. There need be no fear of trawl fishing ever depleting the sea here.
I draw particular attention to that last statement.
The conditions on this side of the Atlantic are altogether different from those on the other. In European waters, in the comparatively narrow North Sea, excessive fishing goes on from January to December by an immense fleet of trawling and other vessels, and in spite of this, the total landings, as has been seen, are actually increasing rather than diminishing. In Canadian waters, on the other hand, and even on the Grand Banks -and this should be kept in view when placing restrictions on trawling here. Owing to climatic conditions there is an enforced close time of at least three months in each year, during which little or no fishing of any kind takes place, and during which even the operations of steam trawlers would be practically stopped. Indeed the Gulf of St. Lawrence, that immense fish breeding area, is practically closed to fishing from December to May, 59 that the fishing grounds, even if excessively worked on during the open season, would, owing to the long rest, soon become replenished. It is, therefore, inconceivable that trawling can develop to such a degree on this side of the Atlantic as ever appreciably to diminish the extraordinary abundance of certain classes of fish such as cod and haddock in the waters of Canada, and I think we may rest assured that its fisheries will remain a splendid heritage for all time.
I quote further from page 377:
I think it is now beyond a doubt that trawling has come to stay here, and although its development will, of necessity, be slow, nevertheless, looking to the time when Canada will have many more millions of people within her borders than she now has, when railway rates have been reduced, and the distributing facilities will have been increased to keep pace with the expanding trade, I believe there will be seen a fleet of Canadian steam trawlers running in from the Atlantic grounds with daily supplies of wholesome fresh food fish.
Mr. Cowie is evidently reconciled to the continuance of steam trawling. He is an officer of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and as such his words carry weight and may be said to reflect the views of the heads of that department, for they have not been repudiated by the minister.
I must say that, taking into consideration this statement of the expert of the department-I do not know whether he is merely an expert or whether he is something akin to a prophet because he seems to be usurping the functions of a prophet when he says that the fisheries upon the Atlantic coast are not going to diminish- together with what I might call the remissness of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in not taking more active steps towards devising some means for the protection of the fishermen, and the fisheries, I cannot do otherwise than come to the conclusion that the minister himself is not very much impressed with the necessity for taking any such step as that. The minister, in referring to this said in effect that unless total prohibition could be obtained the best thing to do would toe to arrive at an agreement based on the North Sea Convention. I think that was the statement that the minister made. He is not in his place so I cannot ask him whether it is or not. I do not understand what he means by that except it be that unless the different countries, France and the United States, for example, are willing to unite with Canada and agree to certain regulations which will prevent the operation of these steam trawlers outside the three-mile limit, he does not know that Canada can go any further than to prevent the operation of them within the three-mile limit. In other words, nothing further can be done than that which has already been done. The minister seems to me to take an erroneous view of the matter when he says that it would place Canadian fishermen and the fishing interests at a disadvantage to take a step, with regard to the framing of the regulations, which would actually prevent the landing of fish caught by these trawlers at Canadian ports. He says that it would work out in this way, that while Canadians would be debarred from the privilege of operating these steam trawlers, Americans, under the new regulations with respect to the charge for the modus vivendi licenses, if the agreement now under consideration should pass, would come to our ports, take these fish outside the three-mile limit, carry them to the American markets and Canadians would be debarred from sharing in that profitable business. I am led to say in reply to this that, if my memory serves, a somewhat similar condition confronted the administration of the department of Marine and Fisheries a number of years ago prior to 1896. The question

was whether or not parse seining should be permitted. I believe that the fishery branch of the Canadian government, made several attempts at a conference with the United States with respect to this, and while the government of Canada contend that purse seining should be prohibited the government of the United States was not prepared to go as far as that, the result being that they could reach no agreement. Canada decided that in so far as Canada was concerned purse seining was to be disallowed. Regulations were passed which did prohibit the use of purse seines by Canadian fishermen. The United States have since agreed to this in the treaty waters. I think that to-day the question is : Is the Minister of Marine and Fisheries doing all that he should do? It is no use for us to go to others and say 'we want you to agree to certain stringent regulations * unless we are able to say that we ourselves have set our house in order. It is not worth while to ask the United States government to agree to something that we have not done ourselves, I object altogether to the United States having anything to do with the policy of the Canadian government with respect to the fisheries. It seems to me that there is too much of this deferring to the United States when it comes to dealing with our own fisheries. We are having too many joint agreements with them, too many international commissions with respect not only to our fisheries but to our waterways. Now, it is our railways. Practically we have come to the point where it is a question of the United States arranging our tariff for us. All these things should be worked out on Canadian lines, and I think the government of Canada should set a high standard if they want others to follow. I do not believe that the Canadian fishermen would find any fault with the government for saying that steam trawling should not be permitted, and I think the Canadian government should take every means it possibly can to prevent the operation of steam trawling in Canadian waters and outside of Canadian waters, and to do that by preventing the ships from landing their fares at Canadian ports.

But the minister omitted to state one very important thing which had led up to this condition. He should have gone a little further and explained that in the year 1907 the government of Canada increased the duty on fish from half a cent to one cent a pound; making it the same as that charged by the United States. It was that very measure, together with the assistance in the payment of the transportation charges which gave the Canadian fishermen on the Atlantic coast, entrance into the Canadian market as far as western Ontario. I remember that in the year 1906, when the commission known as the tariff commission, consisting _ of the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) and the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) visited Nova Scotia, I had the honour of appearing before them at the town of Middleton representing the fishing interests of the county that I have now the honour to represent in this House. I then pointed out to the Tariff Commission that the fact of the United States having a duty of one cent a pound on fish as against our half cent a pound gave them control of our upper Canadian market, and that it was largely supplied from Portland, Gloucester and Boston ; also that the transportation rates were very high and that the chance of getting Canadian-caught fish in the upper Canadian market under the then existing conditions was practically nil.
I was pleased at a later date to see that the government had taken the steps to which I have alluded, and I wish to point out the results in the way of increased shipments from the maritime provinces to our Canadian markets. I wish, in closing, to give to the House a description of one of these steam trawlers and its methods of operation. I shall quote an extract from the New York ' Syren,' quoted by Mr. M. H. Nickerson, M.P.P. for Shelburne in the local legislature in 1909. The extract reads:
The second largest trawler built this year by Messrs. Cochrane & Sons, of Bologne, was launched recently from their ship-building yard at Selby, the ' Canada ' by name. She is described as the largest trawler afloat, and, in fact, is five feet longer than the ' Notre Dame des Dunes.' Her principle dimensions are 156 feet long, 26 feet broad, 15 feet deep moulded, and she will be fitted with powerful triple expansion engines by Messrs. Amos & Smith, of Hull, having cylinders fifteen inches, 25 inches and 42 inches by 27 inches, with a large boiler 15 by 10, and 180 pounds pressure. She has been specially constructed for the Newfoundland fishery, having large trawl winches to contain 1,000 fathoms of warp on each drum. She has also steam windlass, electric light throughout, isolated fish rooms, and in every respect has been fitted up in the most up-to-date manner for deep-sea fishing. Messrs. Wales, Dove and Company's well known bitumastic enamel has been applied to the bottom fore and aft ballast tanks, cabin, engine and boiler spacongs, bunkers, fish room, feed tank, forecastle, store rooms and plates. We understand that Messrs. Coehrane & Sons have in hand a similar vessel for Portuguese owners. Mons. J. Huret is probably the owner of the ' Canada.' He has a number of trawlers engaged in the bank fishery.
The operation of the trawl is thus described:
This trawl was an immense bag of netting, say 100 feet in length and perhaps longer in some of the latter devices, with a very wide mouth or opening on each side of which there was a board, a short wooden wall, resting on the bottom, and between them were stretched two strong ropes forming the upper and the under edge of the mouth, to which the twine was attached. There was a rope from each of these boards to a drum, to the bow and to the stern of the ship. The whole apparatus is dragged slowly along over the bottom while the ship is under headway. The same action caused the mouth to open wide, ~ while the netting took in the fish. It could easily be seen that this device would enclose a multitude of ground fish, such as cod and haddock, and like varieties wherever found. When it bagged them it was hauled up by a powerful steam winch and the contents taken on board. When the catch was large the weight of the huge mass killed the fish and often coral and sharp stones were mixed with the fish, which only helped to bruise them more. The worst feature about it was that it destroyed a large
number of small fish, which, on account of their size, were not saleable, but if allowed to grow would be saleable. It was like cropping the field before the harvest was ripe, something which would be deprecated on land was looked upon as a great stroke of business at sea.
That was in the spring of 1909, and I understand from the minister that since 1908 the number of French trawlers around Newfoundland has increased from 8 to 29, so it will be seen that this method of fishing is in vogue to an alarming extent; that wealthy interests are building up this business, that it is working to the detriment of the small individual fishermen, that the fisheries are being injured by it, that the spawning grounds are being disturbed and damaged, that the fishermen are having their gear destroyed, with consequent loss of time, that in every respect this trawl fishing must be a constant source of embarrassment to the fisherman and of injury to the fisheries.
I cannot use words stronger than those used by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Crosby) in urging on the government the necessity of taking some steps which will effectually prohibit the operation of these vessels in Canadian waters and the landing in Canadian ports of fish caught by them. If we take that stand we will meet with the approval of fishermen throughout the maritime provinces. It may be that a large interest here and there will be prejudicially affected, but I believe that on the whole the end will justify the means; that the fisheries will be conserved and that the interests of the fishermen, which are worthy of the best consideration which can be bestowed on them by this House, will be benefited. The government should protect the poor and hard-working fishermen; the men who are rich enough to build expensive steam trawlers can always protect themselves. I urge on the minister and the House that some steps be taken to protect the Atlantic fisheries of Canada by preventing the landing of fish caught in the trawls at Canadian ports and prohibiting within the three-mile limit the operation of these steam trawlers. The minister has the fisheries protection service fleet at his disposal for that purpose, and under the order in council of 1908 he has power to prohibit their operations. We have the statement of the hon. member for Inverness (Mr. Chisholm) that these vessels have been operating within the three-mile limit and altogether we have a position that calls for prompt and energetic action on the part of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and I trust that such action will be taken.

I am greatly pleased with the wav my resolution has been received by the minister and by the hon. members who have spoken. I was sorry

my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Crosby) should feel that I had not treated him courteously.

I beg to apologize. I did not know at the time I made that statement that notice had been given to the Conservative whips, and I am quite willing to apologize. I thought we had a right to know in advance that this was coming on, and was not aware that notice had been given.

I am quite satisfied with my hon. friend's explanation. This resolution was placed on the Order Paper on the 22nd of November, and it was, of course, open to every member to find out on what day it would be discussed; and, as a matter of fact, the whip of the party asked me if I intended going on with the discussion, and I said I did. I supposed that hon. gentlemen who were interested in the resolution would keep themselves posted in this respect. Permit me for a moment to make reference to the remarks of my hon. friend from Kings. P.E.I. (Mr. Fraser), about the new regulation under which American vessels are allowed to obtain a license for $1 in place of the old rate. My hon. friend seemed to infer that that meant that the American vessels have obtained some fishing privileges which they had not before ih Canadian waters. As I understand the regulation, that is not the case. They have exactly the same privileges that they had formerly under the old license, the only difference being that whereas under the old regulation they paid $1.50 a ton in order to get a license, now they will pay the nominal sum of $1 in order to get a license. My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Crosby) was somewhat excited in his speech, and showed himself anxious, or at least willing, to make this a political question. I would be sorry if we had any polities in a question of this kind. I think we ought to be able to agree on some regulation that would meet the circumstances, and I will gladly join in any reasonable proposal which my hon. friend can make that I would consider effective. I regret, however, that my hon. friend finds it- necessary to blame the government in this matter, because really the government is not to blame. It has dene everything that we could have asked it to do so far. It has prohibited absolutely the use of the trawler in Canadian waters. It has exhausted its jurisdiction so far as that is concerned.

Did not my hon. friend hear the hon. member for Inverness state that the trawlers were operating within the three-mile limit along the coasts of his county? And is he not in favour of the absolute exclusion of steam trawlers by not permitting them to sell their fish in the maritime provinces?

I have not had any such complaint from my constituents. I keep myself very well posted with what is going on in connection with the fisheries of my county, and I can state that the ordeT in council prohibiting the use of trawlers within the inshore waters has been fairly well kept on the coast of my county. Not later than last September I had a meeting at which nearly all the fishermen of Canso were present, and we discussed this matter, but no one made the statement that the trawler had been working within the three-mile limit, and there is no such complaint in any of the petitions from my county that are on file.
Are the fishermen of the county of Guysborough perfectly satisfied with the condition of things at the present time?

No, they are not satisfied. They would like to drive the trawlers off the shore altogether, and I sympathize with them in that desire, and if my hon. friend can show me any practical way in which we can control this matter better than we have been doing I shall be glad to assist him.
I have suggested a way in which it can be controlled-by the government prohibiting the sale of fish from these steam trawlers in the maritime provinces.

That is a proposal that may be worth considering, but the hon. gentleman has not answered the minister's objection to it, that it would simply drive the business to the United States. By doing that you cannot stop the fishing; *you can only stop the sale on the coasts of Canada, and the consequence would be that these trawlers would catch the fish outside the three-mile limit, take them to Boston, and from there ship them to Canada. .What we want is not to stop the sale of fish in Nova Scotia-that is a very poor proposal-but to stop that method of catching fish. We do not want to drive the fish past our own coast and build up the markets of some foreign nation.

I will answer the Minister of Marine and Fisheries now. I believe the fishermen of the maritime provinces know more about their business than either the hon. member for Guysborough or the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and therefore I take their unanimous decision in favour of absolutely excluding from the maritime provinces the steam trawler, or the beam trawler, and I ask my hon. friend if the people of his county do not desire to prevent the steam trawler selling a pound of fish in the maritime provinces.

Mr. Speaker, you have heard the answer the hon. member has made to the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and if you are satisfied with his logic I suppose you will be convinced. The hon. member also made a proposal which I suppose will be regarded by the Halifax 'Herald' of to-morrow as a brand-new proposal coming from himself; that is, that a patrol boat be put on the coast in order to protect the fishermen from the sudden storms that come in the winter season. My hon. friend is not very well posted as to what is going on along the coasts of Canada, or he would know that some weeks ago a patrol boat was placed at the point where most of the winter fishing is going on. I refer to the steamer ' 33,' which has been doing patrol work at Canso. My hon. friend comes to-day with his proposal, after this boat has been put on the patrol grounds by the government, and has done certain work, and he brings in this proposal as if it were now made for the first time.
The hon. minister said that some further investigation should be made, and some officer should be sent on board these vessels to make an investigation. I do not think that will be effective. We shall have to do something more. We would require to adopt the same system as is adopted in Great Britain, and do some experimental work ourselves. The government should take steps to find out for themselves how many of these fish are undersized and whether this trawling system is really a destructive method or not. I question if they could get at the correct facts by sending an officer on board one of these ships. The hon. member for Digby (Mr. Jameson) seems to want to improve my resolution by saying that these trawlers should be prohibited from all the grounds on which fishing is carried on. I would be quite willing to agree if I thought a resolution would be effective; but the reason why I confine myself to what is described as spawning grounds, is that I wish to have a resolution adopted which will be acceptable, not only to the Canadian government, but to the governments of the United States, and Great Britain and France. If we can point out to all these that it is important in the international interests that the fish should be preserved by protecting the spawning grounds, we might get their consent to regulations for that purpose. My idea is that, in confining the resolution to the spawning grounds, it is more likely to be accepted by foreign governments than the one suggested by my hon. friend. I think the hon. gentleman ought to be more cheerful, a^d give credit to the present government for what it has done for the fishermen. I shall not take time just now to go into that matter, because that would be a
very long story, but both my hon. friend and the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Crosby) are well aware what a splendid record this government has had in the last fourteen years with regard to the fishermen. All my hon. friends have to do is to travel along the coast, and see tne large number of breakwaters built to protect the fishermens' boats, expenditures, I may say, which were very severely criticised by some of the hon. gentlemen opposite. Let them consider again the large number of lighthouses erected, and the large number of buoys placed in the different harbours and bays, and the number of wharfs built and steamship subsidies to carry the fish to market. The fact that a freight train has been put on the road between Nova Scotia and Montreal to carry fish at low rate and high speed is something my hon. friends ought to 'bear in mind. All these things have been of the greatest benefit to the fishermen of the maritime provinces.
I regret that my hon. friends should look at this from a political standpoint, but I am glad to know that they will unite with me to-night in the vote, and I hope that something material will result. I trust that we may succeed in obtaining international regulations which will prohibit steam trawlers from operating in the gulf of St. Lawrence and on the banks.
Motion agreed to.
